We will explore the advantages and limitations of each approach and the possibility of merging them to achieve an effective solution.

In 2019, we revised the GP 2 programming language and runtime environment to enhance data structure support, root finding algorithms, and overall performance. GP 2 is a graph parallel programming platform built on top of the Chirp array programming language and runtime, which is used to design and execute high-performance array programs on vast datasets spread across multiple machines. In this study, we introduced BigArray, a new data structure for BigArrays, enhancing array program performance by an average of 1.7 times. To boost the performance of essential array programs like Squeeze, MapReduce, and Sort, we developed BigAlgo, a set of algorithms based on BigArray. As a result, BigArray enabled a 2.1 times speedup in a real-world application for ranking web domains based on their popularity. Furthermore, we integrated BigArray and BigAlgo into the GP 2 runtime environment to significantly enhance graph program performance by an average of 1.4 times.

Our framework combines a unified, end-to-end approach to handle both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction, leveraging a single pre-trained model. It initially employs a self-supervised technique, involving a self-generated mask and corresponding mask prediction network, to learn robust image representations. Building on this, the framework utilizes either a single or multiple labels to refine the learned features. It can also work with either coarse-grained or fine-grained labels. In unsupervised feature learning, the framework refines its encoder by optimizing a feature disentanglement loss, avoiding the need for task-related target labels. In supervised low-shot feature learning, it incorporates a target adapter and leverages a source domain as a reference, incorporating both target labels and source labels to refine the encoder and adapter, again, avoiding the need for target target labels. In supervised fine-grained feature learning, it employs an target attention network and fine-grained target labels to filter out background interference, allowing the framework to focus on target target objects and refine the encoder with both source and target target labels, avoiding the need for target target target labels. Our framework was evaluated in three tasks: unsupervised domain adaptation, unsupervised low-shot domain adaptation, and unsupervised fine-grained domain adaptation. The results showed the framework achieved the best performance in all three tasks.

We have created several infinite sequences of bounded-degree graphs with massive automorphism groups, in both specific and general forms, whose automorphism groups are isomorphic to $\mathrm{GL} n\mathbb{R} q$, for both characteristic 2 and odd prime fields $\mathbb{F} q$, respectively. Additionally, our first all-degree-preserving families are detailed in this study.

A new type of penalized least squares estimator called the Group Lasso is being proposed for both continuous and categorical data. This type of estimator uses a penalty based on the group of coefficients, which the model shares in common. It has the ability to achieve a type of model compression by eliminating redundant parameters and producing a sparse model. The group lasso can also aid in model interpretability by automatically identifying and eliminating unimportant submodels. The group lasso algorithm is being analyzed for its statistical properties and performance under the cve 2022-4288 vulnerability. Specifically, its oracle properties and a consistent variable selection ability under the conditions of $\ell_0$-concave group regularization are being analytically examined. Furthermore, an efficient coordinate descent algorithm for computation is being proposed. The study's results, along with numerical experiments, are provided to validate the theoretical findings.

Recent developments in pre-training language models on specialized datasets have improved their performance in various language tasks. Building on this trend, we investigate the pre-training of fact-knowledgeable language models using knowledge graphs. Our pre-training method extracts factual triples and relation paths from the knowledge graph, forming a structured dataset. We then employ a BERT-based model to train on this dataset. Our model, FactBert, learns to represent entities as sequences of factual statements. FactBert's pre-training on these statements enables it to answer complex, compositional questions about the knowledge graph, outperforming its BERT counterpart by 10.2% and 16.1% on two test sets. However, we also observe that models pre-trained this way are less effective at handling low-hanging-fruit entities with explicit descriptions in the knowledge graph.

This paper explores the connection between nonlocal and classical PDE models, focusing on a specific class of diffusion models with delta-kernel interactions. We analyze the limit of these nonlocal models as they approach local behavior, examining gradients of functions in this limit. Additionally, we derive a corresponding Sobolev-type inequality for this class of models.

Traditional panoramic stitching methods using images can be accelerated by incorporating inertial measurement unit (IMUs). The accuracy of this process depends heavily on data fusion algorithms, machine learning models, and sensor quality. Deep learning has shown promise in improving sensor data accuracy, but current approaches have limitations. We introduce a novel end-to-end learning framework, StreamPanorama, that utilizes continuous inertial data and a single image to generate panoramic views. Our framework is simplicity-driven, utilizing an inertial measurement unit to capture motion and estimate scene geometry. We propose a compact neural network model that learns to map 3D points from the scene to panoramic coordinates. The result is an efficient, transparent system that outperforms existing methods in evaluation benchmarks. The framework's compact architecture can be executed on embedded systems, enabling real-time data acquisition and processing. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by comparing it to state-of-the-art methods and providing extensions for improved results.

We work within a split, simple, linear algebraic group defined over the rational numbers, with the properties of being of type $A$, $C$, or a non-Artin-Galois (non-AG) $E_6$. For weyl group cosets, we establish a successful, explicit formula for combining degenerate Eisenstein series within an $SO(p,q)$ (real) group setting, utilizing the Rallis inner product mechanism.

Parkinson's Disease (PD) is characterized by abnormal oscillations in the basal ganglia, a group of brain structures, and is treated with deep brain stimulation. Building on this, researchers are applying brain-inspired computing concepts to create computational models that can process and predict data, and potentially adapt to changes in neural networks, offering a promising approach to personalizing PD treatments. This paper begins by reviewing current understanding of the disease, then explores relevant computing principles, and finally discusses how these concepts can be utilized to develop effective, adaptable DBS strategies for PD.

To visualize basic metric and histogram data effectively, loom diagrams combine LOCs and donut diagrams, featuring curved line segments with unique join styles. However, existing join method implementations are complex and computationally expensive due to path construction using cubic Bezier curves. For LOOM diagrams, this study introduces a streamlined approach to calculating fan-shaped join parameters and outlines the underlying mathematical principles. This donut join calculation method is efficiently executable on graphics processing units and eliminates unnecessary curve approximations, utilizing straight-line segments instead. Furthermore, this method enhances join style consistency when adjusting data values that influence loom diagram curve radii.

The role of galaxy mergers in the evolution of galaxies and their supermassive black holes is likely significant based on recent observations of outflows driven by active black holes. A statistical analysis of a large sample of X-ray sources was conducted to determine the connection between galaxy mergers and accretion events around black holes. Researchers found evidence of a correlation between the two, particularly in events where the galaxy merger rate exceeded the general merger rate for massive galaxies. The analysis also revealed that outflows may contribute significantly to the suppression of star formation in a substantial portion of events where the galaxy merger rate exceeds the merger rate. The results highlight the importance of considering outflows and galaxy mergers in understanding the co-evolution of black holes and their host galaxies.

A novel type of quasi-interpolation based on a specific family of minimal radial basis functions has been developed, and it possesses properties of preserving convexity and monotonicity. This paper defines the new radial basis function, explores its basic characteristics, and demonstrates how the quasi-interpolation formula can be reduced to traditional M4 interpolation under specific conditions. Additionally, mathematical analysis is used to investigate the monotonicity of the function and its relationship with the generation of new extrema.

Deep learning methods, particularly those utilizing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have excelled in computer vision tasks.  Despite their success, the practical application of these methods is hindered by the need for vast amounts of annotated training data.  To overcome this challenge, researchers have explored various data augmentation techniques to enhance the performance of CNNs.  In this paper, a new augmentation technique called Super Pixel Delimiting Mask (SPDM) is introduced, which involves segmenting an image into distinct regions and annotating them with masks.  The SPDM technique is shown to be highly effective at enhancing the performance of CNNs with minimal computational cost.  The proposed method is demonstrated on the CIFAR-10 and PASCAL VOC 2012 datasets, where the results indicate that the SPDM technique achieves significant improvements in classification accuracy and mean average precision (mAP) metrics.  The effectiveness of the SPDM technique is further validated through the use of mask attention maps generated by CNNs, which provide insight into the model's decision-making process.  The experiments conducted show that the SPDM technique is particularly beneficial for challenging classification tasks, such as distinguishing between birds and airplanes.  The findings of this research have important implications for the application of deep learning methods in computer vision tasks, where annotated data is often limited.  The results of the experiments conducted in this research are supported by supplementary materials available online, which provide additional details and visualizations of the experiments conducted.

Speech enhancement is a vital technology that serves numerous societal purposes.  One effective method of achieving speech enhancement is by creating speech masks through deep learning.  Speech masks can then be used to recover speech by element-wise multiplication.  In this study, we propose a novel deep learning model called the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), which is based on the integration of convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks.  The DPCRN network is composed of two distinct sub-networks, each with its own role in enhancing speech.  Specifically, the first sub-network (EP-Net) is responsible for extracting time-frequency features from noisy speech, while the second sub-network (SM-Net) is used to generate speech masks from the extracted features.  To enhance the speech mask and ultimately improve speech quality, DPCRN employs a multi-scale pooling mechanism, a mask prediction module, a batch normalization layer, and an activation function.  Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the DPCRN model over the existing state-of-the-art models in terms of speech quality, as measured by the PESQ and MOS metrics.

The effective field theory (EFT) of dark energy introduces numerous functions of time and scale that characterize modified gravity models. By analyzing the turn-around radii of rich galaxy clusters within the N-body simulations, we can constrain these functions of modified gravity models, specifically the time-dependent function $\mu(k,\mathcal{H})$. Research into multi-EFT models reveals significant statistical differences ($\gtrsim 3\sigma$) in the turn-around radii ratios at $z=0$, which can be used to break the dark sector degeneracy in $\left\{\Lambda_{\rm DE},\mu(k,\mathcal{H}),\Gamma(k,\mathcal{H})\right\}$ families of models. Additionally, functions of position and wave number in linear multi-EFT models were investigated. Results indicate that the current dataset primarily constrains the combination of these functions rather than each function individually. Consequently, the current dataset primarily constrains the $\left\{\Lambda_{\rm DE},\mu(k,\mathcal{H})\right\}$ family of models rather than multi-parameter space. Ultimately, functions of time and scale can be constrained non-degenerately by combining the turn-around radii with the growth factor of the matter power spectrum.

A newly devised, straightforward two-fluid model is presented which is effective at forecasting the complex interplay of radiative and matter-based heat transfer during Rayleigh-B\'enard convection. By representing the fluid as two components with varying temperatures and being confined between horizontal plates, we are able to accurately replicate results from numerous computer simulations of high-Rayleigh and high-primitive unit cell convection, yielding a consistent $R_a^{-1/2}$ scaling for the $<q^*>$ flux. Notably, our model's predictions of $<q^*>$ as a function of $R_a$ and $\Gamma$ are supported by recently released data from direct numerical simulations, providing further evidence of its reliability.

We investigate the interaction between light and matter in a cavity, specifically the entanglement between the cavity and an atom that was previously separate, and how this interaction could potentially create entanglement among multiple atoms. Our research shows that a photon-adding operation within the cavity can create more entanglement among the atoms than would be possible through interactions alone. The success of this method in creating entanglement is influenced by both the degree of entanglement already present within the cavity and the position of the atoms relative to each other. Furthermore, we utilize a spontaneous photon emission process to create entanglement among multiple atoms, taking into account the entanglement that already exists within the cavity. The entanglement created as a result of this process is comparable to that created when the cavity interacts with multiple atoms during their time inside the cavity. Additionally, we examine the effects of spontaneous photon emission on the creation of entanglement in a diagrammatic model, and demonstrate that the method is resilient to the effects of the CPMR process, even in the presence of actual physical process noise.

This report details the advancements made to the CMS silicon pixel detector between 2015 and 2016, which enhanced the detector's performance and allowed it to process data at a luminosity of up to $200~\mu b^{-1} s^{-1}$. Initially, the pixel detector was upgraded with a new layer of forward pixels and a layer of barrel pixels, but it was subsequently overhauled with a new layer of medium and a new high-level trigger and data acquisition system in 2016. These upgrades allowed the pixel detector to keep up with the increased data rates resulting from the upgrade to the LHC in 2016.

Using the AdS/BHC correspondence, the structure of the glueball spectrum is analyzed with an emphasis on higher resonances. A review of recent advancements in calculating baryon and meson spectral patterns via AdS/CMT correspondence is also presented, and implications for experimental validation are explored. Initial applications to the meson and baryon spectrum are examined, and further research directions are outlined.

Social media platforms offer a vast amount of data that can be easily accessible and are suitable for conducting comprehensive, low-cost studies on public opinion. However, automated systems struggle to analyze this data due to the complexity of the language used in online communications, which often differs from standard written language. In this study, various deep learning techniques were assessed for their ability to accurately determine the sentiment expressed in Twitter messages. The best-performing configuration involved a pre-trained LSTM model that was further fine-tuned using a small, manually annotated dataset of Instagram comments and a larger, freely available dataset of Twitter messages. The resulting system's performance was on par with the leading commercial solutions used by companies to gauge the sentiment expressed in social media posts.

A non-linear analysis of Yang-Mills theory in AdS space is applied to study back-reaction in the context of the large-N limit, leading to an investigation of how a black hole's "shadow radius" and "thermal profile" are affected. The research reveals that a specific non-linear charge parameter influences the shadow radius linearly, in line with earlier findings, while also affecting the black hole's temperature in a non-linear manner. Further analysis leads to an estimation of two specific charge parameters based on strong coupling limits of theories like QCD, which in turn provide insights into the charge operators that influence the AdS black hole's properties.

A new approach to quantum state characterization is proposed, based on a fundamental approach to probability theory. This method is applied to evaluate coherent and squeezed states of the parabolic band model, yielding probability distributions of model observables. The results show that characteristic features, such as nonclassical effects and entanglement variations, can be directly evident in these probability distributions, which are derived from the measurement of model phase space coordinates from optical tomograms. The study reveals the presence of nonclassical correlations and entanglement fluctuations, specifically demonstrating 1D entanglement reductions and 2D entanglement fluctuations in composite systems. The correlations and entanglement variations can be quantified using Kleyra's entanglement reduction and conditional probabilities, which are shown to be feasible in practice. The feasibility of this approach is supported by the experimental availability of the necessary data for analyzing the parabolic band model. The findings are applicable to a broad range of quantum states and systems, providing a practical and informative tool for assessing nonclassical phenomena and entanglement dynamics.

The success of using BERT-based models in dialogue understanding relies heavily on providing them with relevant context through contextual inputs. Determining which context to include is a crucial yet challenging step. We propose a method called Self-Self Improvement (SSI) that uses a bilevel optimization framework to identify the most useful context features for improving model performance. At the lower level, a neural network optimizes a given set of self-selected context features for a dialogue turn, while at the higher level, an agent that specifies roles uses a self-specification reward function to evaluate the effectiveness of these features. Through multiple iterations, both levels converge to provide the best context for the BERT-based model. Our experiments on two natural dialogue datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SSI, with the learned context features and role specifications significantly outperforming random and self-chosen specifications, resulting in a 5.44% boost in BERT-based model performance.

A significant financial burden on farmers arises from the unpredictability of agricultural yields and prices, which are heavily influenced by disease prevalence in crops like strawberries. This study develops a stochastic model to model the pressure of diseases on strawberry yields, and proposes a control strategy to mitigate this pressure. The proposed strategy involves using real-time monitoring and predictive modeling to optimize the use of pesticides, balancing the costs of these inputs with the potential losses in profit due to disease pressure. Results demonstrate that this strategy can reduce the pressure of diseases on yields, leading to an increase in profit, and is adaptable to other agricultural crops.

As 5G technology becomes a reality, high-quality immersive videos will be
accessible through head-mounted displays, offering users a new level of visual
experience. However, loading these large files can cause noticeable delays. To
address this issue, we've developed an innovative approach to loading immersive
videos by predicting the user's field of view and only loading visible parts of
the video. To enhance loading performance, we've found that incorporating video
subtitles as side information significantly improves our approach. By using a
dual-stream architecture, we combine audio tracks and video subtitles to build
upon existing encoder features and achieve more accurate Fovea predictions. Our
method's effectiveness has been demonstrated through comprehensive experiments,
which have yielded a 15.25% improvement in prediction accuracy and reduced
loading time by up to 50% compared to traditional approaches.

We have developed a precise and versatile approach for employing projected entangled state operators (PEPOs) to simulate the effects of thermal conditions and time on one-dimensional systems that consist of interacting particles. By constructing PEPOs in such a way that their complexity only grows linearly with the size of the system, we can accurately represent these systems' outcomes under thermal conditions and the effects of time. Through an efficient algorithm for simplifying PEPOs, we found that their inherent details can be reliably extracted, leading to our method's success in simulating both thermal conditions and times for various models of interacting particles, particularly in finding their steady states.

We examine the decoupling phenomenon for canonical surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with non-vanishing Gaussian curvature, employing a method that integrates Taylor-based local curvature expansion and a expansion of canonical surfaces in tangent planes. A similar strategy is also explored for the decoupling of general smooth surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

Anisotropic $L_p$ capacity and volume inequalities are presented for functions with restricted gradient in an anisotropic Newtonian $R^{n+1}$ space, where the capacity and volume inequalities are tailored to the specific orientation of the given $L_p$ capacity and volume within the $R^{n+1}$ space, with the $L_p$ capacity and volume inequalities reflecting the specific $R^{n+1}$ space's characteristics, with the $L_p$ capacity and volume within the $R^{n+1}$ space being specific to the given $L_p$ capacity and volume within the anisotropic $R^{n+1}$ space, with the $L_p$ capacity and volume within the anisotropic $R^{n+1}$ space being specific to the given $L_p$ capacity and volume within the $R^{n+1}$ space, with the $L_p$ capacity and volume within the $R^{n+1}$ space being specific to the given $L_p$ capacity and volume within the anisotropic $R^{n+1}$ space, with the $L_p$ capacity and volume within the anisotropic $R^{n+1}$ space being specific to the given $L_p$ capacity and volume within the $R^{n+1}$ space, with the $L_p$ capacity and volume within the $R^{n+1}$ space being specific to the given $L_p$ capacity

In measuring accelerations in the Space Experiment for Probing Dark Energy, unexplained fluctuations called glitches appear periodically. These glitches, with a typical magnitude of $10^{-11}$ m/s$^2$, are significantly larger than typical noise and often persist for several hours. They seem to occur at regular intervals, with a frequency of about 11 cycles per day, and are linked to the 3-axis stable mode of the satellite. Glitches are characterized by sudden, unmodelled force fluctuations in the experiment, with an average value of roughly $3\times 10^{-11}$ nN. Their effects are most pronounced on the satellite's diagonal axis, with an average glitch size of about $6\times 10^{-11}$ m/s$^2$. Furthermore, the 13 cycles per day orbital frequency influences the data, with the 11 cycles per day mode of glitches affecting the experiment's three axes. Ultimately, the force fluctuations during glitches are not caused by the sun or moon, but could be influenced by the 3-axis stable mode of the satellite.

A novel class of self-propelled dimers has been discovered, existing between more complex and simpler self-propelled structures.  Researchers found that these dimers exhibit a unique method of motion, where a "ratchet" mechanism causes a step-like progression, analogous to a "ratchet and pawl" design used in gears and clocks.  The study reveals that an asymmetric component is spontaneously selected and drives the dimmer's forward movement.

We investigate a specific two-bead system that achieves self-propulsion through a mix of strongly and weakly hydrodynamic forces. A computational analysis of flow patterns around the beads identifies a strategy for creating net self-propulsion in a solvent, despite the absence of net force or torque.  The research discovers that the motion of these active dimers involves a form of "directional control," where varying levels of mechanical resistance result in altered swimming paths, reminiscent of turning a steering wheel in cars or submarines.

A fundamental network design problem, known as k-strong shortest path cover, involves selecting up to k disjoint shortest paths between a set of source-destination pairs that cover all specified destination nodes, where the chosen paths must be mutually non-sharing except at source nodes. This study makes several key contributions. Firstly, it proves that k strong shortest path cover is NP-hard for any fixed k greater than or equal to 2. Secondly, it explores various special cases and provides exact algorithms, along with complexity analyses. Additionally, it presents heuristic algorithms and conducts computational experiments to evaluate their performance.

Using the global Q^2 evolution equation for structure functions, we calculated the gluon distribution in two models: the BFKL equation and the Balitsky-Levin-Vysotsky (BLV) equation in the leading logarithmic approximation. Calculated average hadron masses from the gluon distribution revealed a significant positive renormalon singularity at $x=1/2$ in both models, with a $O(1/R)$ ambiguity in the nucleon mass estimate resulting from the renormalon, specifically an 8% uncertainty for a factorization scale of 3 GeV. However, no such singularity was found in the structure function $F_2$. Although both BFKL and BLV equations are known to be non-perturbative, we found that the gluon distribution estimates given by the two equations are essentially the same in the leading logarithmic approximation.

We investigate the relationship between a tree's structure and the frog model's behavior, specifically, we establish that there exists a critical degree $d_\mathcal{T}$ for each infinite tree $\mathcal{T}$, where the model shifts from transient to recurrent behavior at this degree. We further identify that the critical degree equals the maximum degree of the tree if it's not hyperbolic, whereas it's strictly less for hyperbolic trees.

We theoretically analyze the interference between surface plasmons and a Rayleigh anomaly in a magnetophotonic structure. A rayleigh wedge is employed to guide surface plasmons towards the sample edge. By calculating the magnetic optical spectrum of surface plasmons, we can attribute specific spectral lines to either the Rayleigh anomaly or surface plasmons. An additional line arises from the interacting anomalies and plasmons. We confirm this approach by observing an line shift caused by varying the angle of the rayleigh wedge.

Knowledge distillation is typically an efficient process that facilitates the creation of a compact model mirroring the performance of a larger one. In this research, we focus on a specific type of knowledge distillation known as decision-based, which is restricted to outputting the final classification results. Our investigation into DB3 has been hindered by a significant vulnerability, where the black-box black knowledge is made accessible by an individual with privileged access to the input data and neural network internals. To address this issue, we propose a novel DB3 approach that relies solely on publicly available decision labels. Our experiments, conducted on privately labeled datasets, reveal that the proposed approach can successfully replicate the compressed neural network's behavior, showing significantly less classification error compared to alternatives utilizing privileged information.

The uncertainties linked to hadronic components affecting normalization and chromospin corrections have a combined standard uncertainty of 3%. This translates to an absolute uncertainty of $1.6 \times 10^{-4}$ for the ratio $\mathcal{B}(B^+ \to K^+ K^0) / \mathcal{B}(B^+ \to K^+ K^+ K^-)$.

Given a module $M$ within the category of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ with high multiplicity, specifically $2m$, and possessing a single factor appearing $2m$ times, and denoting $M_\lambda$ as a module of dimension $\lambda$, we aim to recreate the intricate lattice of submodules of $M$ using only basic information from $M$ itself. Notably, the dimension of $M$ alone is insufficient for this reconstruction, but by incorporating additional data such as local multiplicities, collection multiplicities, the dimension and dimension vector of the quotient module $M^{1q}$, and potentially more, we can successfully rebuild $Sub(M)$. The recovery of $Sub(M)$ holds significant value, as it paves the way for the reconstruction of the submodule lattice of an irreducible $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_n)$-module, which in turn may offer valuable insights into the categorification of the positive part of the quantum homogeneous coordinate ring of the Grassmannian, denoted $QGr_{k,n}^+$.

The Strong Geodetic Recognition Problem involves determining whether a specific subset of vertices in a graph is the unique strong geodetic set. Researchers recently discovered that this problem is NP-complete for general graphs and trees. In this study, we investigate additional graph classes to understand which properties facilitate or hinder efficient solution of the problem. Specifically, we show that Strong Geodetic Recognition remains NP-complete for chordal graphs, even when limited to certain types of split graphs. Additionally, we provide an algorithm with a complexity of O(n^5) to identify all minimal superset sets within a given graph, and we develop an alternative algorithm with a complexity of O(n^3) for apomorphic graphs.

A key imitation learning challenge lies in the large number of training samples required, particularly when an expert demonstration is noisy. We present a new method, iNnocation-Active Imitation Learning (TRAIL), which is an active imitation learning algorithm that is based on introducing perturbations. TRAIL is able to reduce the number of training samples required by identifying state actions that are particularly difficult to learn from the current policy, then requesting a demonstration of those specific state actions, then introducing a demonstration of those specific actions. We theoretically prove that TRAIL guarantees a certain level of performance relative to the number of additional demonstrations provided, and we also demonstrate the efficacy of TRAIL through a variety of tasks using the MuJoCo simulator.

In Co-Imitation Learning, multiple robot experts collaborate to achieve a shared goal, utilizing only their individual action histories for training, rather than relying on expert demonstrations. This concept is effectively applied to tasks like Co-Skills Acquisition, where the goal is to develop a compact set of skills from the raw actions of several experts. By training without expert demonstrations and instead learning a coherent joint policy from the observed action trajectories, the resulting skill set can be used to execute complex, multi-agent collaborations, such as joint object manipulation. This study presents the first co-learning framework based on Generative Adversarial Models, specifically a Generative Joint-Skills Network (GJSN) that jointly trains the joint action policy and joint-skill distribution using only action observations.

Depending on the choice of a cutoff rate to polarized decoder cutoff rates for bias, either the likelihood of a decoder making an error approaches zero, or the maximum code capacity approaches 1 bit per channel use. It is shown that using a cutoff rate of one yields a probability of incorrect decoding that is exponential in the square root of a certain factor divided by n, where n represents the number of codeword elements. On the other hand, using a cutoff rate of zero results in successful decoding behavior that is polynomial in n. The research conducted here provides evidence of the optimal cutoff rate to be approximately 0.0866, where it is confirmed that a sequential decoder can achieve any positive rate of error reduction. The results presented here build upon the foundation of a factor of two from a previous study conducted by Gamal and Wigger in 2016.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has seen significant advancements in various tasks, yet the action space size can pose a challenge, particularly in tasks with vast action spaces like text-based tasks. Our research indicates that optimizing the action space in RL-based reinforcement learning-based machine translation models leads to notable improvements in performance. We propose a range of action space reduction techniques, with the 'retrieval' method emerging as the most effective. The 'retrieval' method is easily adaptable to different models and achieves substantial gains over other approaches, ultimately delivering a 5 improvement in BLEU score on the WMT14 EnDe task when applied to the Transformer model.

This project focuses on an alternative to traditional 3D point cloud-based calibration, utilizing a 2D image-based approach to enhance efficiency and usability.

A novel, straightforward method is introduced, leveraging a depth camera to pinpoint 1D and 2D fiducial markers on a planar target, which can be positioned at various orientations and distances from the camera.

Due to the flexibility in marker placement, this approach is less constrained than conventional techniques.

To guarantee reliability, a statistical analysis is conducted to identify and eliminate outliers from the data set.

A real-world experiment is carried out to validate the proposed method and its results are compared to those of standard solutions.

Key improvements in usability and robustness are achieved, with measurable gains in precision amounting to minimal deviations.

QFS-spaces constitute a novel category of topological structures, which, in conjunction with questionably constructive sets, form a highlyQFS-enriched category. These sets are defined by topological sets whose QFS objects serve as continuous retracts. Notably, a topological structure can be classified as an n-type QFS-space if and only if it is an n-type continuous QFS-retract. Furthermore, a topological structure can be classified as an n-type QFS-space if and only if it is an n-type contractible QFS-space, which in turn is equivalent to being an n-type point.

The extent of polarization present within web hyperlinks has been extensively studied, yet its manifestation within online pages goes beyond link structure, as it is influenced by user browsing preferences which can diverge from hyperlink suggestions. Leveraging a PISA survey that enabled users to browse the web while completing politically neutral search tasks, we gathered unique insights into the discrepancy between users' browsing behavior and the structure of the web itself. While the extent of this discrepancy varies among individuals, we found evidence of it being more pronounced in the political ideologies of users, a difference of nearly half a standard deviation existing between the content of pages users accessed and the web itself. Furthermore, we observed users' ideological preferences to be quite distinct when navigating the web, varying by nearly one full standard deviation between the content of pages they visited, thereby indicating a significant gap between users' browsing habits and the structure of the web itself.

We propose a method for enabling mutual information exchange between a quantum device and its environment without a mediating controller. Based on two fundamental principles - reciprocity and wave impedance matching - we design systems capable of achieving this interaction. First, we apply these principles to create simple linear circuits that facilitate bidirectional coupling. Next, we extend our approach to systems with microscale and nanoscale dimensions, showing that our designs remain effective in these contexts. We simulate the performance of such systems and demonstrate their potential for enabling interactive communication with users and quantum devices.

In our analysis of biharmonic hypersurfaces within Euclidean (n+1)-dimensional space, we examine the effects of minimum recurrence on biharmonic hypersurfaces that are not totally umbilical. Specifically, we find that the recurrence of an operator significantly influences the configuration of these hypersurfaces. Notably, when the second Laplacian is applied to the shape operator and it results in a minimal biharmonic hypersurface within Euclidean space, we demonstrate that the given setup is only feasible for the case of totally umbilical hypersurfaces. Moreover, we establish a non-totally umbilical approach and prove that a biharmonic hypersurface that is not totally umbilical is possible under the condition of an irreducible recurrent shape operator and a recurrence parameter of 2.

Given two coprime integers p and q with p greater than q, we examine the base-p recognisability of subsets defined using base-p recognisable sets in the power of N_p/q, the set of base-p integers without zero digits. Additionally, we characterise p/q-recognisable subsets of N_p/q's d-power (for any d greater than or equal to 1) by introducing the concept of p/q-automata and showing equivalence with these new automata.

The strongly interacting U(1)暗色模型, 或简称为U(1)MSM, 已经成功解释了几个谜团, 如强力的CP问题和中微子的质量起源. 然而, 它仍然存在一个未解决的问题, 即电弱真空的不稳定性. 为了解决这个问题, 我们在U(1)MSM中添加了两个标量场和一个中微子的右旋态, 创建了新的模型auMSM. 通过仔细分析, 我们发现仅仅引入右旋中微子就会使电弱真空变得不稳定, 但加入两个标量场后, 模型能够稳定中微子的质量矩阵的最小值并解决中微子的终极中衰变问题. 我们还研究了新的标量场对自发电弱真空衰变和单能希格斯衰变到暗色胶子的影响. 通过对比单能希格斯衰变到双胶子的实验数据和理论数据, 我们发现约束很宽松. 对于单能希格斯衰变到一暗色玻色子一标准模型希格斯玻色子的情况, 我们得到了更严格的限制. 此外, 我们确定了模型参数空间, 以满足中微子振荡数据和中微子终极中衰变数据, 并预测了几个在未来的对撞机和中微子实验中可检验的量.

The LAMOST time-domain survey, spanning from 2020 to 2022, involved 18 fields and 550 individual visits, resulting in the observation of over 12 million individual sources and a total of 3.2 billion spectra. In response to the demands of variable star discovery, we conducted an in-depth analysis of the data processing, reduction, and construction of a new catalog of binary star candidates generated by the LAMOST time-domain survey. Each binary spectrum underwent meticulous quality control measures to ensure its reliability. After filtering out low-quality entries, the final catalog comprised 85,000 binary star candidates with spectra of sufficient quality. A detailed examination of the catalog's characteristics, including mass ratios and separation distances, was carried out and presented. A quality assessment of the catalog was performed through the identification of well-documented binary systems within it. A notable discovery included the catalog's inclusion of $\v$~Pup, a well-known visual binary with two distinct components of 9.5 and 10.5 magnitudes. Additionally, three new binary systems with orbital periods of less than one day were identified as potential candidates for further study.

Convolutional Neural Networks, or CNNs, are extensively used in image analysis due to their impressive performance.  However, their effectiveness can be hindered by the loss of precise positional information during the pooling layers.  To address this issue, EG-CNNs, or Edge-Gated CNNs, were developed by inserting additional pooling layers with edge-gating mechanisms that retain and guide the retention of border information.  Experimental evaluations on the MICRS and PASCAL VOC datasets using the PConv implementation revealed that EG-CNNs outperformed standard CNNs and Convolutional Pooling CNNs in terms of Dice Coefficient and Mean Intersection over Union (IoU) metrics.  Notably, the EG-CNNs achieved superior results in retaining information about image objects located near the edges.

We have analyzed the concurrency control mechanisms of MongoDB 4.0, pinpointing the exact instance where it surpasses traditional snapshot isolation guarantees. By defining three distinct configurations of the S7 model that account for MongoDB's non-reentrant lock usage and its decentralized architecture, we have demonstrated that WIREDTIGER, a modified form of snapshot isolation, is satisfied by standard MongoDB deployments. On the other hand, we found that attempts to utilize timelines with conflicting write sets, stricter read set requirements, or read sets that include committed but unapplied writes, will fail. Notably, we found that non-standard behaviors described in the MongoDB documentation, including reads that bypass locks on collection documents, are justified and predictable outcomes of its read-modify-write protocol, which we found interesting given the collection-level lock strategy it employs.

This paper establishes that the $e$-positivity of $chro(yDy)$ holds for every Dyck path $D$, 
extending a prior result by Jojiya and Solus. Additionally, the $q$-positivity of $chro(yDy)$ 
is explored, with specific focus on identifying conditions under which $q$-positivity is maintained 
when $D$ is not multiplied by $y$.

When a learner attends to specific inputs, it may be beneficial to summarize the consequences of those inputs in a way that minimizes attended prediction errors. When the attended inputs are uncorrelated, a novel hindsight summary learning algorithm can derive valuable information from the resulting hindsight data to form effective summaries. This algorithm's capability to produce useful summary information extends to scenarios where the attended inputs exhibit correlations. Notably, the algorithm's performance in these scenarios is comparable to the optimal performance achievable with direct, unfiltered experience. When applied to a set of ball-tracing paths in a grid world, the algorithm learned compact spatial representations of the trajectories' locations and actions, thereby generating useful hindsight data. This data, in turn, enabled the algorithm to accurately predict errors in unvisited areas of the grid world.

A significant concern with using image data to train deep learning models is the presence of implicit biases within the training sets, which can hinder a model's ability to generalize effectively, particularly in medical image analysis. Although techniques exist to measure bias and develop fair algorithms, there's a lack of such methods for endoscopy images. In this study, we introduce a new endoscope benchmark and conduct an in-depth analysis to identify implicit biases in these images. Our findings reveal significant correlations between classification outcomes and various patient demographics such as age, gender, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status. Moreover, we explore and compare various countermeasures to mitigate these biases. Our results suggest that implicit biases in implicit data are often task-specific and can be mitigated to an extent, but complete elimination proves challenging.

We examine the phase diagram of a network of triangular structures where Ising spins are interconnected through three distinct types of bonds. This analysis is conducted using an exact high-temperature expansion method. The coexistence of first and second order phase transitions is found to arise from the interplay between three-state Potts models (embedded within the triangles) and Ising models (embedded at the network's centers). The phase diagram displays multiple scenarios depending on the relative interaction strengths between the models. Furthermore, the relationship between these interactions and the profile of the hysteresis loop is determined. A dual model is also proposed for this system, along with an explanation of its features.

A comprehensive analysis of solar coronal holes has been carried out using SOHO/LASCO data from 1998 to 2008. The study focused on 1.5 million solar eruptions that occurred within 0.316 to 1 AU, with a particular emphasis on the energy necessary to overcome the Sun's gravitational pull at these distances. The results revealed that this energy follows a power law distribution in the described range, albeit with altered characteristics at 1 AU. The results further indicated that magnetic energy available in coronal holes is sufficient to initiate the observed energetic releases at both small heliocentric distances and 1 AU. In addition, the energetic releases appear to be more strongly related to potential magnetic energy as we move away from 1 AU. Finally, the findings suggest that the energetic releases at small heliocentric distances are not significantly impacted by interplanetary shocks.

This study introduces a novel neural architecture, a multi-task neural network with shared attention mechanisms, for the automatic detection of textual emotions. The model effectively integrates features from multiple language-related emotion recognition tasks using dynamic attention mechanisms that are trained end-to-end. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, particularly in its ability to adapt to new and unseen languages through the development of emotion-related attention mechanisms. The authors' experiments confirm the superiority of their model over existing methods, with the attention mechanism achieving the best performance on both related and unrelated corpus examples. The source code for the attention-based neural network is openly accessible on GitHub.

Bi5FeTi3O15 (BIFT) is an interesting Aurivillius compound that has been studied extensively. Researchers have previously determined its complex layered structure, which consists of multiple perovskite blocks separated by slabs of biorthogonal structure. Studies have also shown that BIFT exhibits distinct dielectric properties, displaying both paraelectric and ferroelectric behavior. In this study, we have investigated the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of BIFT under the influence of hydrostatic pressure using first-principles calculations. Our findings indicate that under pressure, the unit cell volume decreases, and the unit cell parameters converge, ultimately leading to a phase transition from a P3ma structure to an Amm2 structure at around 18.5 GPa. Under high pressure, the material undergoes a transition to an insulating state, characterized by a large band gap of over 2 eV. In the high-pressure Amm2 structure, the material exhibits a large magnetic anisotropy energy of over 100 meV, and the Fe ions exhibit predominant magnetic anisotropy.

This paper explores the use of discrete paths in robotics and related fields as approximations of optimal continuous trajectories. A key concern is addressing error bound issues, which can be mitigated by localized error bound computation. However, this approach comes with challenges, particularly in determining the discrepancy between a given discrete path and the optimal continuous trajectories it represents. Using bounded variation functions to define a specific class of optimal trajectories, we use the variation of constants method to prove that the error between these trajectories can be bounded, thereby providing a foundation for our main proof. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the global error bound of a discrete path compared to the optimal continuous trajectories is not excessively large, assuming certain conditions such as convexity and compactness are met.

A recently discovered phenomenon, known as the Glaser effect, has occurred in a laboratory setting involving a shock wave propagating through an ideal gas. Under specific conditions, approximately 150 microseconds after entering a low-pressure region, the wave develops an internal compression region known as a rare shock. This research aims to theoretically analyze various types of shocks and identify conditions for the emergence of rare shocks. By applying conservation laws and examining characteristics of shocks and Mach cones, we have developed an empirical formula for the location of the rare shock's onset. Additionally, our findings suggest that the onset location is influenced by several factors, including post-onset gas velocity, pre-onset shock velocity, and the adiabatic exponent of the main shock. Analyzing the Glaser effect specifically, we determined that a rare shock will form if the adiabatic power of the main shock exceeds a critical value, with the estimated onset location being around 250-300 millimeters, potentially limited by the size of the experimental apparatus.

We compare the Caprini, Leellouch and Neubert (CLN) and Boyd, Grinstein and Lebed (BGL) parametrizations for hadron $B\to D\pi$ decay rates. Although both frameworks are rooted in the same fundamental principles, the BGL parametrization offers a distinct mathematical expression from the CLN one. Given the limited experimental data available to fit these two types of parametrizations, it is difficult to draw definitive conclusions about which provides a more accurate fit. Nonetheless, given the nature of both types of parametrizations, it is expected that with more experimental data available in the future, the large standard deviations associated with these fits will decrease, potentially revealing any discrepancies between the two. We also examine the relationship between these two types of parametrizations and find that the size of the differences between them depends on the location of the pion pole in the complex plane.

In one dimension, supersymmetric quantum non-singular potentials exhibit a unique property: their associated polynomial Heisenberg algebra has exactly one unit of excitation. This characteristic becomes particularly useful in understanding the relationship between SUSY oscillators and the harmonic oscillator. By applying a chain of SUSY transformations denoted as $\mathcal{S}$, we can map the Hamiltonian of an $N$-fold SUSY oscillator directly to that of the harmonic oscillator. As a result, the polynomial Heisenberg algebra for the $N$-fold SUSY oscillator is found to be equivalent to that of the harmonic oscillator in terms of its unit unitarity.

A novel approach to studying chaos in dynamical systems is introduced through the concept of a Lyapunov graph, which can be used to calculate the Lyapunov exponent and show that certain systems possess a specific invariant measure that is locally ergodic and entropy-measuring in a topological sense. This framework is applied to verify the positive entropy of the R\"{u}ssell-Horsley Polednik-Weiss map and the full, slow full $\y$-expansion of the interval map.

Researchers are studying the switching and escaping phenomena in superconducting circuits with junctions in mind, as understanding these processes is essential for developing faster and more energy-efficient quantum circuits. We have conducted experiments on asymmetric superconducting loops, or SQUIDs, consisting of one large and one small junction, investigating how different configurations affect the switching current in relation to an applied magnetic field. By varying the widths of the Josephson junctions in our samples, we observed the role of phase synchronization between the junctions on the switching current, showing both increased and decreased values compared to a single junction. We have also observed the impact of phase synchronization on the current-voltage characteristics of the superconducting circuits, and we have found that our findings can be explained using a classical resistive-capacitive Josephson model.

A new approach to calculating the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law, Casimir energy and pressure is presented, based on finite temperature field theory and real-time formalism. This method is applied to an abelian theory, specifically QED in $M^3\times S^3$, to calculate the Casimir energy and pressure using the non-abelian aether term and the GLPT. The results show that both calculations yield the same outcome, which is then used to explore the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and Casimir energy.

The complex nature of the HJR3 contract necessitates a robust model for calculating its value and the associated risk of mispricing. In this study, we enhance the previously used 3-factors affine intensity jump model by adding a third factor model and compute the contract's value and expected unhedged payment obstacle under the new model. An integration expression is derived for the expected hedging difficulty before implementing any hedging strategy, which, when compared to the results of a Monte Carlo simulation, exhibits a high degree of accuracy. The advantage of this integration formula lies in its computational efficiency, offering a significantly faster calculation time than the Monte Carlo simulation method. The computation time using the integration formula is roughly 1/1000th of the time it takes with a Monte Carlo simulation, which can be computed on a personal computer within a second. Additionally, an analytical approximation for the default probability of the reference entity is presented, which matches the Monte Carlo simulation results with a high degree of accuracy. The approximation results in a simple quadratic equation that can be solved to find the desired probability.

This final report seeks to comprehensively explore the potential for applying calculus of variations principles to analyze complex, heterogeneous materials that are subject to linear differential equations. The focus is on understanding the behavior of functional analysis in these settings and investigating the mechanisms of homogenization. A key aspect involves examining the optimal homogenization techniques, particularly those involving the use of periodic structures and multi-scale analyses. The outcome is a detailed framework for deriving effective, homogeneous models that accurately describe the material's overall response. The presentation will culminate in a concise summary of the findings and an overview of promising areas for further research.

We've developed an improved method for identifying tidal structures in images based on the work of Zucker. By using the GAMA survey and HST images of early-type galaxies, we assessed our algorithm's performance in detecting specific features like tidal tails, shells, streams, and globular clusters. Our study revealed a clear relationship between a galaxy's mass and the presence of tidal features, with more massive galaxies having a higher likelihood of exhibiting these structures. Specifically, we found that shells and streams occur more frequently in very massive galaxies, while globular clusters are evenly distributed across galaxies of different masses. Additionally, we discovered that smaller galaxies with a host stream or tail tend to be located in the lower-mass range. Our findings also support the idea that tidal features are typically associated with satellite galaxies rather than being a common occurrence among massive galaxies.

Minor modifications in opportunity distribution can lead to substantial, far-reaching effects on future generations' socioeconomic prospects, based on a novel mathematical model. This model examines how opportunity distribution influences future generations, resulting in both intergenerational inequality and spatial inequality. A key policy suggestion is made to mitigate these inequalities.

Laser systems based on nonlinear optics and photonics are becoming increasingly common in various applications, making their accurate and efficient simulation crucial. Despite the availability of numerous numerical methods for modeling these complex systems, none offer a comprehensive solution that can handle a broad spectrum of applications. This is partly due to the diverse nature of NLO-based systems, which complicates the development of a unified approach for their simulation. This paper presents an algorithm that accurately models the characteristics of ultrashort pulses and efficiently simulates NLO systems using the discrete variable representation (DVR) method, which can be applied to both linear and nonlinear optical processes. By leveraging the adaptive DVR (ADVR) technique, the method minimizes memory usage and enables the development of an open-source Python library called NLO-ADVR for the simulation of NLO-based systems and ultrashort pulses.

A recent study has revealed that the scaled unit ball in the L_p^n space, for any n greater than or equal to 3, cannot have an epsilon-isometric dimension reduction by linear operators when the space is not a Hilbert space, meaning it is not the L_2^n space. This research has confirmed this property for the L_p^n space under different conditions for p, including (1,4) and its dual interval (p',4). Notably, the end of this interval has been examined but not fully proved. This article has established that line operators fail to have an epsilon-isometric dimension reduction for the scaled unit ball in the L_p^n space, for all p in the interval (1,infinity), and all n greater than or equal to 3.

The beam-beam interaction at the Large Hadron Linear Collider (CLIC) results in a significant closed orbit distortion at the point of interaction of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). This effect is directly linked to bite-sized beam interactions and cannot be eliminated due to the inability to separate beam interactions at the LHC. Consequently, beam beam closed orbit differences have a direct impact on IP-LHC bite-sized beam interactions and cannot be separated from them due to limited diagnostic capabilities. To mitigate this effect, we explore various strategies involving the design of the CLIC interaction region and potential modifications to the closed orbit in the beam pipe. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of these strategies on chromaticity correction and non-linear beam optics. Furthermore, we discuss strategies to mitigate closed orbit differences in the beam pipe by potential solutions such as shifting the beam interactions, correcting the orbit in the beam pipe, or installing orbit diagnostic capabilities in the beam pipe. Finally, we present optimized optical solutions along with corresponding correction strategies to ensure satisfactory beam optics performance.

This paper addresses a critical issue in distributed optimization where malicious agents disrupt communication by disrupting the transmission of gradient vectors. We tackle this problem by analyzing an iterative algorithm that agents use to maintain communication and solve a common convex minimization problem. By assessing the time complexity of the algorithm under various communication attack scenarios, we determine its robustness and effectiveness in the presence of these disruptions.

To achieve the full potential of upcoming cosmological instruments like the Euclid satellite and the LSST, we must first understand and account for various instrumental systematic errors that can distort our measurements of the universe's expansion and structure. One effective method to do this is to create realistic computer simulations of these effects and test the ability of data analysis techniques to recover accurate cosmic parameters. In this presentation, the aim is to provide researchers in the field of cosmology with an open-source computer code library to generate high-quality simulations of these instrumental errors. The code will be based on established Python packages such as astropy, astropy-mosaic, and astropy-cosmological parameters, and it will be user-friendly through an interface called astropy-volcalitas. The quality and realism of the simulations will be ensured through the collaboration of experts who have shared their knowledge through the Euclid-EFT collaboration. The proposed code will be a crucial step in preparing for the analysis of cosmic parameters from the data collected by these instruments, as it will allow us to accurately estimate and correct for these systematic errors through the use of likelihood models. The researchers will share their plans for the future of this code, as it will be made available to the public through an interface on GitHub. The code will be an essential tool for the Euclid-EFT collaboration, as it will be used to analyze the data collected by this instrument and to develop new methods for estimating and correcting for these systematic errors. The collaboration will be led by

The task of determining the correct linear order of words from an unstructured set is a challenging yet fundamental problem in linguistics. Recent studies have utilized the Ambiguous Word Order (AWO) dataset to evaluate machine learning models' ability to predict linearized orders, assess ambiguous sentence interpretations, and assess the effectiveness of attention-based models in parsing. This paper addresses the difficulty of current AWO models by examining their limited ability to generate partial tree structures that represent syntactic dependencies. Given the prevalence of such representations in syntactic analysis, we investigate the task of partial tree linearization and assess the efficacy of these models in this context. Although not as challenging as the partial tree linearization task, our experiments using the more straightforward AWO sentences reveal that the models struggle to produce accurate outputs with significantly higher error rates compared to their performance in predicting linear word orders. Furthermore, we modified an attention-based model into the Boundary Attention Model (BaM) tailored for partial tree linearization by incorporating additional attention mechanisms to predict dependency relations and identify phrase boundaries. Despite the significant differences in task complexity and evaluation metrics, BaM's performance in linearizing partial trees from unstructured sentences is comparable to the original AWO model's performance in linearizing words.

Global feature alignment is a key difficulty in developing Deepfake detection networks that function properly across different domains. To tackle this challenge and create an effective Deepfake detection network capable of functioning in various domains, we propose two novel techniques for connecting network layers: multi-scale cross-stitch connections and domain-adaptive cross-stitch connections. The first method enhances performance by integrating features from different scales, while minimizing the cross-stitch module's complexity through adaptive filter domain adaptation in the second technique. It directs domain-adaptive connections to achieve optimal performance with minimal domain-adaptive modules. These cross-stitch modules enhance the detection network by aligning low-level domain differences and global features. The experiment results show the effectiveness of the proposed methods over simple alignment methods, and our Multi-CA Net achieves superior accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods on multiple datasets.

This paper analyzes the performance of regular LDPC codes on the erasure channel,
examining the impact of neighbor degree correlations in neighbor degree correlations in
various drawing methods, both randomly and in order, on LDPC code success rates. The study
reveals that a negative degree-degree correlation significantly boosts the maximum tolerable
erasure probability by up to 20%, whereas a positive correlation has a negligible impact.
Furthermore, it is discovered that a near-circulant structure in the LDPC code parity-check
matrix yields substantial performance gains over a random structure, resulting in a
~15% increase in the maximum tolerable erasure probability. The proposed LDPC code drawing
technique leverages a negative degree-degree correlation to achieve a 25% improvement in
the maximum tolerable erasure probability, thereby meeting the end-to-end delay constraint
with a maximum delay of just two time slots. A similar analysis based on the Shu et al. threshold
model supports these findings.

We investigated the feasibility of various QKD attacks, considering multiple decoy states, taking into account distinct states' photon numbers and spatial modes. Under the assumption of ideal photon sources, we identified that an eavesdropper could execute a vacuum+weak decoy state attack, where only the weak decoy state measurement appears legitimate. This attack becomes feasible when the vacuum attack threshold photon number ($n_0$) of the weak decoy state is less than the difference between the vacuum attack threshold photon numbers of the single mode decoy states. Similarly, we demonstrated that the multi-mode photon number QKD protocol is vulnerable to a vacuum+weak decoy state attack if the single mode $n_0$ is greater than the multi-mode $n_0$. Our theoretical analysis was validated by simulating the vacuum+weak decoy state attack on the Qiskit QKD system.

This paper explores the potential of optimizing edge computing infrastructure on a smaller scale, considering its geographic distribution and a dynamic demand pattern that changes at different time intervals. Various optimization models are analyzed based on the computation and energy constraints of individual edge servers, as well as the server group constraints, with a focus on minimizing the number of active servers and energy consumption, and improving user latency. Strategies such as linear programming, mixed integer programming, and heuristic methods are evaluated for their effectiveness in reducing energy consumption with little impact on latency, and the results show that a strategy called DEDALUS achieves near-optimal solutions while significantly lowering energy consumption in testing scenarios, with a notable reduction in consumption on a university network.

This paper's conclusion builds on recent findings in geometry and mathematical analysis, as well as new developments in the study of angle functions in metric spaces and manifolds with metric structures. Specifically, it addresses and resolves key challenges in conformally embeddability for spaces featuring Poincaré inequalities and Sobolev inequalities.

This paper formally proves an inequality related to the number isomorphism classes of orders within a fixed number field, specifically those that satisfy a compatible isomorphism with their own endomorphism rings, which scales non-linearly as the field's degree to a power of one-third. Informally, the bound lies between the tenth and twentieth powers to the tenth root. Building on this foundation, we derive both simplified and extended inequalities for non-isomorphic orders, the first strict inequality within the literature to suggest the Non-isomorphic Minkowski Length of degrees between zero and ten is finite. Moreover, the derived inequalities hold true in higher degree fields as well. Additionally, the paper references recent scholarly research conducted in the last decade.

A high-speed nitrogen jet was used to modify the pressure-sensitive paint (PSP) on the rotor blades of a rotating airfoil in order to create pressure gradients. By adjusting the jet's pressure, we were able to determine its effect on the surface interaction and resolve details at a microscale. Pressure sensors, along with the paint, provided data that could be compared and used to validate a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation. The paint's resolution was found to increase with higher jet pressures, but this effect was limited, and the ambient pressure inside the test chamber also played a key role. It was discovered that at lower paint pressures, there was not enough resolution to accurately depict the separation line, and increasing the jet's pressure allowed for better definition. The results from the sensors and the paint were found to be in agreement, and the paint's resolution was found to be limited to a certain point. The research also found that the paint's resolution was affected by the structure of the nitrogen jet, and that the paint's response time was found to be around 10 milliseconds. The research also found that the paint's resolution was affected by the amount of nitrogen that was being used, and that the paint's resolution was found to be around 0.0001 kilopascals. The research also found that the paint's resolution was affected by the amount of time that the paint was exposed to the nitrogen, and that the paint's resolution was found to be around 0

In a protoplanetary disk, self-maintaining planetesimals can form through the aggregation of dust particles driven by the persistent self-propagating (SVP) turbulence.  A detailed analysis of the turbulence reveals that the vortex structure possesses rotating arms, with a rotating arm mode that is responsible for the turbulence's self-sustaining behavior.  A critical threshold of Reynolds number is required for the emergence of self-maintaining vortices, and we establish a mathematical relationship for this requirement.  Our simulations suggest that self-maintaining vortices are capable of producing small-scale planetary bodies, and we estimate a Reynolds number range for their formation, specifically between $10^4$ and $10^5$.  These findings offer a potential pathway for the creation of planetesimals in a protoplanetary disk.

We develop a protocol to identify neutral modes in many-body systems with a linear spectrum, where charge currents decay over time. Our proposed method can identify neutral modes by checking two conditions: the total current in the system is conserved and there are no corresponding quantum links between parts of the system. This method works for various setups, including quantum Hall systems, where the neutral modes persist indefinitely, and systems with focal-point singularities, where they decay rapidly. We demonstrate that our protocol is flexible and can be used to both derive and detect neutral modes in a broader range of settings.

The given work extends a previously established result by Azad and Stolin from the quantum group U_q(g) to the broader setting of the quantum group U_q(g) for any semisimple Lie algebra g within a fixed reduced root system. The previously established basis, denoted as the bar basis, for U_q(g) is shown to be compatible with the Braid group action defined by Lusztig as well as the actions resulting from the simple reflections in the Weyl group. This compatibility ensures that the bar basis maintains its integrity under these actions. Additionally, this research provides explicit formulas for the results of applying these actions to the highest weight vector. A specific formula for applying the long element of the Braid group to the highest weight vector, particularly in the case of the A_n system, is also provided. The compatibility of the basis with Lusztig's action is further shown to facilitate the resolution of an open question initially posed by Geck and Vogan, as well as subsequent inquiries by multiple researchers, regarding the multiplicity-freeness of certain finite Weyl group orbits within the set of nilpotent conjugacy classes of a corresponding classical Lie algebra.

This research investigates the application of decentralized stochastic gradient descent (DR-DSGD) for optimizing a sum of differentiable functions under a distributed framework. In this setup, each of the n individual functions is located on a separate device, and the optimal solution can be achieved with minimal inter-device communication by optimizing only one function per iteration. To evaluate the algorithm's efficiency, we provide a precise convergence rate analysis in a linear model, accounting for both communication and computation costs, and compare its performance to that of standard decentralized stochastic gradient descent. Our findings indicate that DR-DSGD offers significantly reduced communication requirements while incurring negligible computation costs, thereby offering a practical approach for optimizing large-scale machine learning models.

The hard-disk phase-transition scenario has been a subject of study for decades and is now a well-established model for investigating complex transitions between different phases of matter. Despite its apparent simplicity, hard disks present significant challenges due to their discontinuous transition, which is accompanied by multiple intermediate structural states and lacks certain characteristics such as latent heat and symmetry breaking. To gain insight into this phenomenon, researchers have employed a vast parametric study using various order parameters to better understand the nature of the transition. Their findings suggest that hard disk transitions exhibit distinct features that are more closely aligned with "first-order-like" classifications. Furthermore, their results indicate that certain widely used models, such as the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson framework, are not applicable to describing this type of complex transition.

This paper explores the impact of the nuclear parton distribution function (nPDF) on the description of jet characteristics in the context of the LHC. To simulate the jet, the CASCADE PYTHIA model was employed, taking into account the SIBYL-evolved nPDF known as EKS98. Various jet parameters were analyzed in the case of a jet with an anti-kT radius of 0.4 and a jet transverse momentum of 50 to 2000 GeV. The study revealed a significant influence of the nPDF on the jet shape, particularly at large values of the distance from the jet axis, as well as on the distribution of jets, the distribution of the missing transverse energy, and the ratio of the transverse energy within the jet. The findings are in line with the observed data from the LHC for the single-differential distributions of the jet, but the inclusion of the nPDF results in a discrepancy with the experimental measurements for the cross-section of the jet and the ratio of the transverse energy within the jet.

Pyramid schemes, notorious for their deceptive and potentially harmful financial practices, have historically been difficult to study in detail. The 2021 collapse of the Forsage cryptocurrency trading platform, a notorious level 10 pyramid scheme, unexpectedly enabled an in-depth investigation into the behavior of its participants. By leveraging on-chain data and combining it with external sources, researchers analyzed nearly 1.4 million transactions involving approximately $225 million. A key finding was that the vast majority (99.9%) of users suffered financial losses, with around 99.1% losing more than $1000. Moreover, the study revealed that the initial 30 levels of the pyramid, containing nearly 99.9% of its users, consistently operated below its stated level structure, and that the median cost per claimed pyramid level was significantly lower ($2000) than the reported cost ($50000). By examining the intricate relationship between the amount invested, the estimated number of levels, and the reported level structure, investigators were able to gain a deeper understanding of the operational dynamics of high-level cryptocurrency pyramid schemes.

We present new age and metallicity estimates, along with the initial-final mass mapping for the globular cluster candidate GCs in the Milky Way. Utilizing our deep wide-field photometric data spanning the U to K bands, we identified the red giant branch tip in the OGLE-2016-BL-10050000000000000000 object. The age of GCs in NGC 6656, NGC 6752, and NGC 6910 is estimated at 12.6 billion years, 12.4 billion years, and 12.5 billion years respectively. The metallicity of NGC 6656, NGC 6752, and NGC 6910 is estimated at -0.4, -1.3, and -1.4 in the [Fe/H] scale. Our research also provides a comprehensive initial-final mass mapping of these GCs, which can be applied to other astronomical objects.

This study examines the impact of the Higgs boson's non-zero width and various parton distribution function sets on the p_T distribution of the quark-Higgs system. A Gaussian approximation is used to account for the Higgs boson's finite width, and Monte Carlo simulations generated via Excel and ROOT are analyzed. The results show that different PDF sets produce different p_T distributions, with the CT18 set providing the best fit for experimental data due to its incorporation of latest LHC data. Quark-mass effects have a significant influence on the p_T distribution, particularly for heavier masses, with the impact being more pronounced for masses greater than 600 GeV. Furthermore, the research indicates that an 1% precision in p_T data could be achievable at the High-Luminosity LHC.

Researchers have employed tight-binding (TB) models extensively to investigate materials with strong light-matter interactions. However, these models often produce inaccurate results due to issues with the velocity operator within the TB framework. The diagonalization of the Schrödinger equation using TB models typically neglects the Coulomb interaction present in the full many-body problem, frequently omitting configurations where Coulomb blocks are crossed during non-degenerate perturbation theory calculations. To improve accuracy, a method has been proposed that replaces the Coulomb interaction with an effective single-particle potential, commonly known as the self-energy within many-body physics. Furthermore, a unitary transformation has been developed to ensure that off-diagonal elements of the Coulomb interaction in the momentum space are mirrored by corresponding off-diagonal shifts in the kinetic energy within the momentum space, maintaining accuracy consistent with first-order perturbation theory. Applying this method to TB models yields additional terms to the standard 2x2 Hamiltonian matrix used to describe optical transitions between conduction and valence bands. Notably, this unitary transformation is essentially a refined version of the Lee-Low-Pines transformation, widely utilized in many-body physics to eliminate Coulomb interactions within the momentum space.

A tensor network that encodes an erasure correction code can be simplified without losing this functionality, provided its rate and dimension are maintained. We have established comprehensive restrictions for a tensor network composed of a single error-prone tensor that serves as an erasure correction code.
