A novel mechanism to achieve this large discrepancy in transition temperatures is also proposed, in which a specific choice of magnetic materials and thickness can result in spin-dependent transition temperatures. A predicted mechanism to achieve this large discrepancy in spin-dependent transition temperatures is presented, in which a specific combination of magnetic materials and thickness can result in spin-dependent transition temperatures that differ by up to 5.5 K. A model is presented to predict spin-dependent transition temperatures in a Heusler/Ho$_3$Ti$_5$O$_{12}$ heterostructure, in which a large discrepancy in spin-dependent transition temperatures can be achieved. A model is presented to predict spin-dependent transition temperatures in a Heusler/Ho$_3$Ti$_5$O$_{12}$ heter

An advanced statistical model has been developed to predict the interdependence between the spatial arrangement of traffic lights and the flow of vehicles approaching an intersection. This model effectively captures the non-uniform distribution of approaching vehicles and enables predictions based on various parameters, including the effective gap width. To test its accuracy, data from a German freeway was analyzed, focusing on how groupable transmission probabilities change across different locations. The results showed that traditional local models were insufficient, whereas the effective gap width model significantly improved prediction reliability. Furthermore, the study suggests that light-vessel transmission models could be more appropriate in certain scenarios. The proposed effective gap width model is straightforward to implement and aligns with fundamental traffic flow theories, making it a highly relevant and achievable concept for real-world applications.

The calculus of constructions, developed by Benedetti and Castéran in 1990, serves as the foundational system for numerous contemporary theories combining programming and typing. Its simplicity and expressiveness have inspired a significant body of research, resulting in numerous theories of the greatest bounds and an extensive corpus of related work. This survey will explore the fundamental principles of the calculus of constructions and its potential enhancements through various principles such as inductive definitions, higher-known polymorphism, and dependent types.

Quantum electronics has been hindered by a lack of appropriate language and theory to describe and design devices that manipulate and measure entanglement. This situation has changed with the development of multiple correlation functions and especially the link between factorized and measured density matrices. These tools enable quantification of a wide range of electronic states, from coherent and squeezed states to cat states and highly entangled states such as GHZ and graph states. With this approach, we can now calculate the von-Neumann density-matrix entanglement, and a good relationship has been found with the quantum information theory concept of mutual information. Mutual information is particularly useful for analyzing systems with multiple coupled quantum dots.

A nonparametric approach to analyzing data composed of multiple sources is explored through a Bayesian framework. Rather than parameterizing the number of sources, their characteristics, or their individual contributions individually, we define a Dirichlet process prior on the sources' composition. By applying Bayes' theorem, the posterior distribution of sources' contributions can be derived given the observed data. The methodology is validated using both simulated and real-world spectral data, demonstrating accurate estimation of identifiable admixture weights under various model configurations, as well as efficient computation via Gibbs sampling. Notably, our method outperforms existing techniques in terms of computational efficiency.

In the strong-coupling regime, we have achieved calculation of two-loop corrections to certain anomalous dimensions, specifically the quartic and quadratic anomalous dimensions, of a class of twist-four operators within the context of $AdS_5\times S^5$ superstring theory. Our method involves employing the quadratic and quartic terms of the classical energy, derived from the Nambu-Goto action, to directly forecast the corresponding anomalous dimension contributions. This calculation is carried out for configurations in which all quartic contributions are non-vanishing, particularly those featuring one unit of twist in $Z_2$-even sectors. Our calculations confirm the accuracy of prior, numerically obtained boundary conditions, and we have further explored additional sector configurations that were initially conjectured based on duality with a planar limit of $N=4$ super Yang-Mills theory.

The rise of deep learning has led to significant memory demands on GPUs, sometimes exceeding available memory and causing performance issues due to frequent reallocations. The size of neural networks varies greatly, from a few megabytes to over ten gigabytes, making default memory managers ineffective due to their inefficiency and high overhead. Existing solutions like cuMem and GIMMem offer better performance but struggle with very large memory requirements due to limited customization options. We present the DynaSOAr GPU memory allocator, an adaptable memory management system that combines the efficiency of Slab allocators with the low fragmentation and excellent performance of SOAr. The DCAR module within DCAR enables efficient memory area discovery, while the slabs within DCAR provide customized and efficient memory allocation. The results from our evaluations demonstrate that DynaSOAr outperforms the competition in scenarios with large memory needs, particularly when used with popular deep learning frameworks like PyTorch and TensorFlow.

This paper examines the boundedness and compactness of the $p$-Laplacian operator and its potential well as it pertains to the energy functional within specific, recently developed, and tailored function spaces, including those with varying characteristics and structural properties. We explore and analyze the behavior of these operators in a range of and unique function spaces, with an emphasis on their well-defined and measurable aspects, including their well-bounded and compact properties.

Researchers have previously detected single YSR states through a non-local Andreev reflection technique, but this study is unique in observing multiple YSR states generated by a single Fe adatom on a Fe/Cu(111)/Pb interface. By using an electrostatic pen to manipulate the position of a second Fe adatom or dimer, the study demonstrates the ability to control the positions of YSR states based on the spin-orbit coupling strength. The control of the peak positions can be achieved by adjusting the separation of Fe atoms/dimers, the number of Fe atoms in a dimer, and by manipulating the local spin-orbit coupling. The findings provide a pathway to developing a controllable solid-state quantum bit using a single molecule. The study also reveals the influence of a second Fe adatom on the peak asymmetry of the YSR state.

Implicit neural networks have gained popularity in semantic segmentation due to their ability to map input coordinates to pixel values without relying on neighboring pixels. However, this characteristic makes training implicit networks challenging, particularly when aiming for high-resolution outputs. In contrast, implicit Fourier features enable these networks to produce high-resolution outputs at a low computational cost by leveraging the global periodic nature of Fourier transforms. Despite this, current implicit Fourier networks struggle to generate complex shapes, limiting their use in tasks like semantic segmentation. To address these limitations, we introduce FourierMask, the first implicit Fourier network capable of generating detailed semantic segmentation masks. FourierMask combines the implicit Fourier transform with a mask decoder that incorporates both magnitude and phase information from the Fourier features. This decoder, along with implicit Fourier features, allows FourierMask to reconstruct intricate shapes from global pixel-wise pixel information. Additionally, we develop a data augmentation technique tailored to semantic segmentation that improves the network's ability to utilize global information. With this approach, FourierMask achieves cutting-edge performance on multiple challenging datasets including KITTI, SunRC, and Waymo.

We have previously established that the existence of entirely bounded minimal disks in three-dimensional Euclidean space can be completely described, and a similar comprehensive understanding of the minimal annulus within the same space has been achieved. In this study, to expand upon the annulus results, and leveraging a theorem of Pottmann regarding the infinite multiplicities of the Laplace operator on a specific type of minimal surface known as the Enneper surface, we establish a major connection between the completeness of certain, minimally embedded annuli in three-dimensional Euclidean space and the completeness of a specific subset of the Enneper surface, with a particular, prescribed curvature value, within the same space.

Clouds, which cover significant areas of Earth's surface, have a profound impact on our planet's climate system. Analyzing satellite images of the clouds allows researchers to gain a deeper understanding of cloud formations and their effects on the climate. However, interpreting these images can be complicated by the non-Euclidean geometry of the planet's surface. To address this challenge, a new cloud interpretation model has been developed using a spherical geometry framework. This model, which is based on the principles of spherical geometry, divides clouds into three distinct components: a "veiled core" that is hidden from view, a "ring" that is partially obscured, and an "exposed core" that is fully visible. By separating these components, the model is able to classify clouds with a high degree of accuracy. In contrast to traditional methods, which treat clouds as two-dimensional objects, this model takes into account the three-dimensional nature of the planet's surface and provides a more realistic representation of cloud formations. As a result, researchers are now able to analyze clouds in a more comprehensive and accurate manner.

A T-shaped laser pulse, consisting of a main negative chirp and an extremely thin, low-density secondary layer at its short-wavelength end, is found to significantly enhance ion acceleration in a laser-solid interaction. When this secondary layer is present, a strong, ultra-short, over-critical plasma channel is created through the layer itself, which then accelerates ions from the central region of the target via the associated potential. The ions' kinetic energy results from the interaction between the electron layers at the front of the plasma and the central target, which are separated by the fine structure of the T-shaped pulse. Theoretical calculations and particle simulations both confirm the existence of this ion acceleration mechanism. The energy of the accelerated ions is found to be proportional to the intensity of the main pulse and the square root of the target's density, with the proportionality constant being around 85 MeV in this study. The accelerated ions exhibit a narrow energy spread of approximately 10 MeV. The acceleration's magnitude is unaffected by the parameters of the main pulse, as long as they meet certain minimum requirements. The central ion beam's intensity, however, is highly sensitive to the spacing between the two pulse peaks, with the beam's intensity reaching its maximum when the spacing is an integer multiple of the laser's reduced wavelength. The findings suggest that a T-shaped negative chirp laser pulse could be a promising source of high-energy, narrow-spread ion beams with minimal need for target optimization.

Recent astronomical discoveries have identified several systems with multiple planets, yet few contain as many as the 5 transiting mini-Neptunes found in this star system. Three of these planets are located within the star's habitable zone, a region where conditions may be suitable for liquid water to exist. Although these planets are not considered directly habitable due to their size, they are of great interest for the study of water content in exoplanets. Using high-resolution spectroscopy, we analyzed the atmospheric composition of two of these planets, comparing their water content to that of our own solar system's Earth. The comparison revealed the $H_2O$ to SiO$_4$ ratio to be in the range of $10^4$ to $10^6$ times greater than in the solar system, a value that is not constrained by our current understanding of the planets' interiors. The large size of these mini-Neptunes makes their atmospheres more accessible for study with the upcoming James Webb Space Telescope, a tool that could provide valuable insights into the water content of exoplanets.

First we identify stable configurations of impurities in TiO${_2}$, including carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and chlorine in both substitutional and interstitial positions. Utilizing a first-principles approach, we calculate defect formation energies, ionization levels, and charge neutrality levels for all these configurations. We also analyze defect energy levels within the band gap, defect states, and core level shifts. Interstitial carbon and nitrogen exhibit significantly lower formation energies than their substitutional counterparts due to a lower energy cost associated with relaxing Ti atoms. Oxygen and chlorine exhibit similar stability in both positions. Notably, only interstitial carbon can act as a p-type dopant with a low charge neutrality level of 0.26 eV above the valence band maximum. Furthermore, O${_{sub}}$0 and N${_{sub}}$- defects introduce deep energy levels within the band gap, potentially leading to recombination centers that shorten the carrier lifetime.

We set limits for flavor-changing neutral current (FCNC) branching ratios in flavor non-universal semi-elastic processes like $tt\bar{b}$, $tt\bar{c}$, $tb\bar{c}$, and $tt\bar{t}$, resulting from the decay of a single top quark. Using 137 inverse femtobarns of $pp$ collision data at $\sqrt{s}=8$ TeR, we establish limits without referencing other production mechanisms for these final states. The branching ratio limits are found to be $BR(t\to b\bar{c}) < 1.2\%$, $BR(t\to b\bar{c}) < 1.1\%$, $BR(t\to t\bar{t}) < 1.1\%$, and $95\%$ confidence level limits are also set for pair production processes $pp\to tb + X$ and $pp\to ttc + X$.

The intra-cluster medium is a primary component of the universe's hot baryonic matter. Its complex structure and temperature variations can be investigated using a sensitive X-ray microscope, with the X-IFU instrument on the upcoming Athena satellite playing a crucial role. To fully utilise the X-IFU's potential in studying the study of turbulence in the intra-cluster medium, precise theoretical models of a plume-like flow must be developed. Through simulations using the pencil code, researchers have created synthetic X-IFU images of a turbulent plume, focusing on the Fe-K and O-K emission lines. These images reveal distinct features, such as the thickness of the cluster interface, the size of the plume, and the separation between the Fe-K and O-K lines. To gain a deeper understanding of the flow's dynamics, researchers have developed simplified theoretical models, which have been compared to the synthetic X-IFU images. These models have been particularly effective in predicting the O-K line profile, but further analysis is needed to fully reproduce the Fe-K line profile. To further refine these models, more realistic simulations incorporating additional emission lines and their three-dimensional structure are needed.

We establish a generalized version of our previously announced finding, which was based on our answer to a question posed by Faudree and Schelp. For a triangle and its colored edges, we prove that if the graph has a sufficiently high degree, as defined by $\frac{r-1}{2r}\binom{2r}{r}$, it inevitably contains a specific subgraph, specifically the complete graph $K_{2r}$ with at least one edge colored in color $r$.

Investigating isothermal turbulence models, we studied the density anisotropy in the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) using Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) data at high resolution. By analyzing dust continuum and $^{13}$CO line emission at 0.0014 pc scales, we developed an ellipticity index to map density structure. Our results showed that anisotropy in the CMZ varies with scale, with elongation oriented perpendicular to the Galactic plane in the |l| < 30$^{\circ}$ region. Furthermore, our data suggests that small-scale turbulence in the CMZ is influenced by large-scale stellar feedback, channeling it into perpendicular flow. This study highlights the importance of studying high-density, small-scale turbulence in the CMZ to better understand its impact on star formation.

Our proposed system for detecting the presence of eyes is uniquely focused on just the eyes, in contrast to traditional methods that require the entire face. This innovation has the potential to be implemented in a variety of settings, including homes, schools, and public spaces, due to its ability to operate efficiently across different faces and environments. To achieve this level of versatility, we utilize deep learning technology, specifically a pre-trained MobileNet model, to create a compact and fast detector that can run on mobile devices. Furthermore, we enhance the accuracy of this detector by training it on the Y1 dataset, which comprises a comprehensive set of one million labeled images of closed eyes collected from the YouTube website. As a result, our focus-focused detection approach for the presence of eyes demonstrates superior performance, with a mean average precision (mAP) of 93.1%, outperforming the traditional face-focused method while requiring significantly fewer computational resources, as measured by the number of pixels processed.

Researchers investigated the robustness of determining a qudit's mass in the presence of mass-fluctuation errors. While focusing primarily on third-order moments, they also examined relevant second-order moment issues. Their studies encompassed both open and closed quantum systems, specifically examining system-environment interactions through various channel models, including amplitude damping, phase damping, and amplitude-phase damping. Notably, they discovered that a qutrit system is generally less affected by these processes compared to a qubit system. In particular, the mass-determination accuracy of a qutrit is significantly more tolerant to these processes, especially in cases of stochastic processes. They also examined the impact of these processes on the order-reduction tolerance in both open and closed systems, ultimately concluding that the additional energy level in qutrit systems provides a distinct advantage in tolerating the degradation caused by these processes.

Our research successfully created high-energy positrons with a polarization level exceeding 30%, a significant milestone that could enable the development of magnetic positron filters for the muon collider and trmuon projects. In this presentation, we will showcase the current status and forward plans related to the completion of these projects.

We've developed a general framework for the proof that broad categories of groups have polynomial diameter properties. This encompasses finitely generated soluble groups with limited nilpotent subgroup types, GQ-groups consisting of growth-type polynomials in their nilpotent subgroups, and groups with limited nilpotent subgroup types and growth-type polynomials in their conjugacy classes. A key aspect of framework is the definition of function groups, which are those where all nilpotent subgroups adhere to the given polynomial bound. We've demonstrated that several broader classes of groups, including the aforementioned soluble groups, GQ-groups, and groups with limited conjugacy classes, consist of function groups, often with specific polynomial diameter limits.

This research focuses on designing an integrated circuit that can accurately measure temperature using a 180nm CMOS process, operated at 1.8V. The temperature detection system achieves remarkable precision, with a temperature resolution of 0.01°C and the capability to detect minute temperature changes as small as 0.01°C. The project has been successfully completed using the TSMC 1P6M 180nm CMOS fabrication process, with three functional units produced and tested after bonding to a ceramic substrate. The temperature measurement unit's inaccuracy has been found to be within ±2.1°C, and the temperature range it can measure spans from 25°C to 85°C.

Recent findings from our laboratory show that a toroidal magnetic field component can effectively suppress the kink instability in a highly twisted magnetic field when supported by a magnetic twist and a poloidal field component. Conversely, a toroidal field component can suppress the torsional Alfv\'en eigenmode when supported by magnetic twist, but struggles with the kink instability in cases of large twist. The objective of this study is to explore the impact of mutually supporting toroidal and poloidal magnetic field components on the kink instability in the outer region of a twisted torus where the twist is significant. Using linear theory, we analyze the stability of a twisted torus in a twisted toroidal configuration, characterized by a toroidal core surrounded by a twisted magnetic flux tube with a poloidal field component. The results show that for a high toroidal core pressure, a specific balance of twisted flux tube parameters can lead to kink instability suppression even in areas of large magnetic twist. The twisted flux tube's helical twist and helical displacement caused by the poloidal field component play a crucial role in this process. The findings from this study offer a theoretical basis for understanding the behavior of twisted magnetic fields in magnetic stars and twisted magnetic flux tubes in the solar heliosphere.

When exact RG flow equations cannot be solved, their relationship to fluid dynamics provides a useful framework for understanding the inherently irreversible nature of RG flows. This paper derives a general inequality that reflects this irreversibility, much like the second law of thermodynamics in fluid dynamics, and explores its implications for understanding RG flows.

When tasked with finding specific music lyrics or audio, standard web searches can be quite time-consuming. To address this issue, we propose MusicBlox, a specialized search engine that starts with a lyrical description from a user and quickly retrieves relevant music tracks from the web's vast library. We first designed MusicBlox's backend, MusicBlox Box, which handles music lyric data, before moving on to the search engine itself. We evaluated MusicBlox's performance against a standard web search (using Bing) and found that it offered 1.90 to 2.25 times more relevant results with an average of 1.95 relevant results per page, all within the same number of review pages.

Given any topological groupoid $\mathcal{X}$, we assign a corresponding topological stack denoted as $\mathcal{x}$. Topological groupoid extensions are shown to correspond to topological groupoid morphisms that relate to gerbes over topological stacks. Furthermore, the concept of a topological groupoid extension is equated with a specific type of biextension over the underlying topological stacks of the groupoids involved. However, this correspondence is not straightforward due to the distinction between morphisms that preserve the stack structure and those that do not. As an illustration, we examine the relationship between line bundles and the fundamental group of a topological groupoid.

Observations of star formation in nearby galaxies reveal a diverse range of star formation rates associated with individual super star clusters. To understand the formation of massive stars, we combined the physical growth timescales of a sample of star clusters in LMC with their corresponding masses and observed a consistent linear relationship between core mass growth timescales and the resulting star formation rates. This implies that core core masses grow consistently before collapsing into super star clusters, explaining the variability in the final mass of these structures.

This study explores the Godel algebraic structure known as finite Godel algebras of signature three, focusing on their finite variations. It introduces a finite relation called the μ-duality between finite algebras and finite forests, allowing representation as a bipartite graph. The study identifies specific properties of this duality, showing that biμ-dual pairs occur frequently within the category of finite algebras and that every finite algebra corresponds to multiple non-isomorphic forests. It also establishes a unique representation for forest mu-duals and investigates relationships with traditional Godel algebra dualities, finding that the duality is not conjugate but rather an extension of the existing framework.

Similar to 2D images, label-missing 3D point cloud LiDAR data classification is also a common task. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to classify such data by learning from unlabelled neighboring points within a local neighborhood. By leveraging unlabelled neighboring points to provide contextual information around each query point, we can effectively utilize supervised contrastive learning to enhance the representation of query points and improve their classification accuracy. Our method is simple yet effective, and it achieves remarkable performance gains of up to 10% in classification accuracy on commonly used 3D datasets, particularly when the label ratio is as low as 10%. Moreover, our method exhibits greater robustness and reliability when compared to existing approaches. The project can be accessed at https://github.com/zhengqian99/Neighboring-Supervised-Contrastive-Learning.

This study investigates the preservation of positive definiteness in zonal functions on the $n$-dimensional sphere under differentiation and integration operations. Specifically, it determines the limitations on differentiation and the minimum radius of integrability for these functions. This analysis is performed within a framework that uses the representation of positive definite functions on the sphere through Gegenbauer expansions.

Recent research has suggested a potential link between the directions of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays and the locations of neutrino sources, citing the possible correlation as evidence of protons being the primary source of cosmic rays. Considering current constraints on diffuse neutrino excess and UHECR interactions within the source neighborhoods, a significant source-neutrino correlation would necessitate multiple high-flux neutrino sources that emit VEUS or ULAS fluxes while staying consistent with diffuse excess constraints. Such a scenario, however, would result in an apparent correlation in the UHECR distribution due to their greater scattering. In contrast, if a single large source exists, it would be detectable through both UHECRs and neutrinos, resulting in an excess that may be offset by numerous smaller sources contributing to the diffuse fluxes. Such a source would be directly observable, providing evidence of a cosmic ray composition that transitions from protons to heavier nuclei at the knee energy due to the diffusion break's position being determined by the differential source distribution rather than a sudden transition in the source population.

We have developed a quantitative assessment method to evaluate the surface roughness
of liquid foams, which is defined as the root mean square height variation over a
determined area. This method leverages high-speed video footage to quantify the
displacement of a foam boundary as a result of a vibrating object's interaction with
the foam's surface. The resulting measurement of perimeter displacement can be
correlated to area-based roughness measurements via the Haversine Theorem, thus
enabling more accurate assessments. Utilizing this approach, we investigated the
impact of velocity on the roughness factor of a liquid foam, thus providing
experimental evidence of the non-reversibility of this process. Furthermore, this
agreed with theoretical models of irreversible velocity thresholds exhibited by
liquid foams.

Deep learning techniques, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have surpassed traditional methods in the field of image recognition. Despite their impressive performance, there is a growing concern about the reliability of these models, as they often make confident but incorrect predictions. One method to mitigate this issue is the use of ensemble classifiers, which combine multiple classifiers to make more accurate predictions. This paper conducts a comprehensive study of the capabilities of ensemble methods in the context of reliable CNN predictions. The study evaluates different types of ensemble classifiers, including linear and k-nearest neighbors based methods, and compares their performance to common re calibration techniques. The results demonstrate that carefully designed and trained ensemble classifiers can significantly outperform individual CNN predictions and standard re calibration methods in terms of producing accurate confident predictions. Moreover, the study provides a set of open-source codes and datasets to facilitate further research in this field.

The dynamics of incompressible fluid within a rotating Hele-Shaw cell are thoroughly examined using the model developed by Saffman and Taylor. Hele-Shaw flow models featuring singularities and high speeds are replaced with an asymptotically singular and self-similar model known as the One Sheet model. A key characteristic of this model is its ability to exist in either an outer-branch state or an inner-branch state, with a tension-dependent switch between the two states. An inextricable relationship is found between a memory function and the membrane tension, with a tension-membrane balance inextricably linked to yield point stress. Notably, an alternative theory is presented to explain the rate at which a single-sheet membrane can be pulled from the corner of a Hele-Shaw cell.

The average value of dissipated work can be broken down into individual values of work experienced by each unique microstate. Traditional explanations of work's expansiveness rely on multiple instances occurring simultaneously within a system's ensemble. In contrast, it has been found that a single microstate experiences its own additional work component resulting from changes in the Hamiltonian of the system. The concept of partition function's independence from ensemble size led to the conclusion that the internal work component is also experienced by each unique microstate. The total work found in a microstate's configuration space was further divided into an external work component and an internal work component, which was found to be directly related to changes in the Hamiltonian of the system. The relationship between these components was expressed mathematically through the equation $W_{tot} = W_{ext} + W_{int}$, where $W_{int}$ was expressed as $\Delta H$.

We used an advanced statistical method to analyze the line spectra of the Cygnus A molecular cloud and discovered the presence of two unique carbon-based molecules: benzene (C6H6) and cyclopentadiene (C5H5). An inspection of the absorption features in the spectra of Cygnus A revealed the following: the ratio of the absorption features of the two molecules is approximately 1:1, the ratio of the two molecules' gas-phase abundances is approximately 10:1, and the molecules are undergoing a process of photodissociation. An examination of laboratory data revealed that cyclopentadiene can exist in a stable gas phase when subjected to moderate UV radiation. Furthermore, an analysis of gas-phase molecules revealed that the abundance ratio of the two molecules is consistent with an equilibrium between the two molecules that results from a process of unimolecular reaction. An inspection of interstellar absorption features revealed that the ratio of the two molecules is consistent with an equilibrium between the two molecules.

This paper proposes a look-ahead attention mechanism for conventional machine translation models, allowing the attention module to anticipate future input tokens within its current field of view. The look-ahead mechanism is applied to end-to-end neural machine translation models, specifically the attention-based model and the model with residual connections and attention multi-hops. Experimental results on Chinese-to-English machine translation demonstrate that the look-ahead attention module significantly enhances translation performance, particularly for the model with residual connections and the attention multi-hops model. The look-ahead attention mechanism enables better utilization of available information, providing more accurate attention probabilities and allowing the model to plan ahead in terms of output words.

The European Grid Initiative's proposed pan-European grid computing infrastructure has been extensively discussed in the context of a translational approach to technology development and application. This approach, which involves the simultaneous consideration of technology creation and application, is then applied to the development of the European Grid Infrastructure, resulting in the identification of three primary challenges. These challenges are addressed through the design and implementation of a comprehensive infrastructure that comprises three interconnected components: a multifaceted funding structure, a diverse user base, and an integrated value chain.

A new class of quasi-Hubble invariant models is introduced within this study, applying a similar concept to previously proposed models but for the Hubble parameter.  We analyze cyclic and bouncing cosmologies based on this new model, both with and without an anti-de Sitter phase.  We also calculate the coefficient of a scalar tensor model in a de Sitter universe using a Lagrangian similar to the quasi-Hubble invariant model.  We find that the model's parameters can be recovered accurately, provided the universe's expansion rate during the bounce and the current expansion rate are comparable.  We then explore the possibility of recovering the model's parameters in a cold big bounce and the beginning of the next cycle, both with and without an anti-de Sitter phase in between.  The study shows that the model's parameters can be recovered in these scenarios, indicating that quantum gravitational effects and the expansion of the universe could be cyclic.  The research also calculates the number of e-folds in the hot big bang phase and the corresponding temperature.  The study concludes that the model's parameters can be recovered in the next cycle, indicating that the model is consistent with the current observations of the universe.

A longstanding theory suggests that curiosity is an innate human trait, which is now being challenged by our research. We believe that peers play a significant role in influencing an individual's level of curiosity. This idea is reflected in popular culture, where phrases like "being curious around curious people" are used. Such influence might be part of curiosity's evolutionary function, helping us to socialize and learn from each other. We aim to empirically test this hypothesis regarding the peer influence on curiosity. To do so, we collected data from 500 participants in five different countries, who completed a survey in the presence of either curious or noncurious confederates. The results show that participants were more curious when surrounded by curious peers, confirming the peer influence effect. This effect was consistent across all five countries, suggesting that peer influence is a universal aspect of curiosity. Our study contributes to a better understanding of curiosity's underlying mechanisms and its relationship with social behavior.

Our research extends graph Matérn Gaussian processes to support non-integer differential operators, building upon a non-periodic extension of the matrix anisotropic power-law covariance function. By introducing an approximation using the stochastic partial differential equation's solution, the implementation becomes feasible in mini-batch and non-conjugate learning settings, enabling the use of the full posterior for robust uncertainty quantification. Furthermore, the approximation's computational efficiency is enhanced through the integration of the induced probability model's latent Gaussian structure and the use of the induced Gaussian precision model's Cholesky factorization. These improvements facilitate the employment of the full posterior in various settings, and we demonstrate the method's performance through numerical experiments and real-world data applications.

The rapid expansion of cities and the accompanying growth of ridesourcing services present a challenge in effectively monitoring and managing urban road networks through sensing technologies. Unpredictable weather conditions and growing congestion can further limit the reliability of fixed infrastructure-based sensing systems. However, the mobility and widespread distribution of ridesourcing vehicles make them ideal for providing reliable, widespread road monitoring. This paper introduces a innovative approach to designing a cooperative communication network that leverages ridesourcing vehicles for road monitoring, and develops an efficient algorithm to determine the optimal level of participation. Furthermore, it explores the impact of infrastructure capacity on the optimal level of cooperation and introduces a new algorithm to address this issue. The proposed approach and related algorithms were validated through simulations, with the results demonstrating the performance gains in coverage under various network conditions and the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in achieving near-optimal solutions within a limited computational timeframe.

Limits on dark matter interactions with neutrons can be influenced significantly by the apparent disappearance of $J/$psi particles from $J/\psi \tau \to \text{invisible}$ decays, particularly in scenarios involving final final states containing neutrinos. Using shape information from J/psi reconstruction in events with low missing energy in J/pstau decays, we can derive limits on nuclear final states in dark matter scattering off nuclei that are not as restrictive as existing limits set by J/pstau -> invisible decays in nuclear final states with masses between 1 and 10 GeV. These limits, which are obtained from J/pstau -> invisible decays in nuclear final states are 1-2 orders of magnitude more restrictive than existing limits set by J/pstau -> invisible decays in nuclear final states with masses between 1 and 10 GeV. These limits can be improved upon with more data collected in the future at the J/psi peak energy.

Recent research has shown that state-of-the-art second-order linear multistep methods with variable step sizes, known as SGLMs, are highly effective. These methods combine the best features of GLMs and GMs methods by utilizing the difference in the difference of the derivatives at the most recent two steps. We have developed a new SGLM implementation on nonuniform grids, allowing for more flexible and accurate results by interpolating the second derivative differences at each step. Unlike previous SGLM implementations that assumed a uniform grid, this new method does not rely on such an assumption.

The MFSSA technique has successfully showcased various properties and MFSSA will move further by presenting new properties and addressing MFSSA limitations. Two key drawbacks of MFRSSA will also be identified, along with the features of a new technique, MFRCSSA, which will be introduced and key properties of MFRCSSA will be identified. Real-world applications of MFRCSSA will be demonstrated through the analysis of temperature data and image classification using remote sensing.

The rapid advancement of deep-learning technologies has led to the development of essay-scoring models that have achieved impressive performance. However, the inherent biases of these models can result in issues of over-sensitivity and over-stability. To address this concern, our proposed bias-aware scoring model, called BASA, incorporates attention mechanisms and global context to reduce excessive sensitivity and stability. Experimental results demonstrate that BASA outperforms traditional methods, including LSTM and Attention LSTM, resulting in lower sensitivity and stability as well as comparable overall performance.

I introduce a class of heavy-tailed distributions characterized by subexponential properties, then analyze the class's behavior as it approaches extinction, dividing it into two categories based on the parameter 'b'. For values of 'b' greater than or equal to one, the asymptotic behavior of the distribution mirrors that of a regularly varying distribution with a specific tail decay rate. Conversely, values of 'b' less than one result in a different asymptotic behavior, then express the class's tail decay rate in terms of its underlying parameters. Additionally, I provide a detailed description of the right tail behavior for values of 'b' less than one.

A continuous plasma source was created and configured for experimentation, consisting of two parallel plates producing a continuous flow of plasma between them. The plasma's characteristics were assessed using a probe, with experiments varying the plasma's electron temperature, density, and potential, as well as a series of flow rate adjustments. The results showed that plasma parameters were interdependent and that the density could be adjusted to specific levels within a defined range. The data obtained from the experiments were used to develop a simplified mathematical model of the plasma source that accounted for the effects of the plasma's potential and could be further refined.

The use of biological control methods with entomopathogenic nematodes has been
successfully employed for a variety of pests, including the Japanese beetle.
However, implementing these strategies effectively requires a thorough analysis
of the dynamics at play, taking into account the life cycle of the insects, as
traditional methods often fail to do so. In response, we developed a mathematical
model that incorporates the full life cycle of the insects, and used it to develop
vaccination thresholds for achieving disease-free equilibrium. Our model's
results align with our intuition, in that nematodes can only be considered
effective when they exceed a certain infection rate, and that the beetle's mating
period plays a crucial role in determining when this threshold is met. Furthermore,
we identified that nematodes can only be considered successful when they push the
beetle's maturation period past a certain point, and that varying the duration
of this period can lead to a decrease in the beetle's population, and even cause
the population to decline indefinitely, thus providing a valuable insight into
how nematodes can be used to effectively control pest populations.

A nucleus detection task in digital pathology is challenging due to the vast number of nuclei present in tissue samples, the similar appearance of the nuclei, and their clustered distribution. Existing research has primarily relied on convolutional neural networks for this task. We introduce a novel W-shaped network architecture that incorporates two parallel detection modules and an intermediate fusion process. The unique design of the network facilitates efficient learning of local and global nuclear features. The framework is particularly suited for closely spaced objects with similar appearances. Experimental results on three publicly available datasets demonstrate the superiority of the W-shaped network over state-of-the-art methods, the benefits of its unique architecture, and the feasibility of enhancing the network's performance through the proposed fusion process. The code is available at the provided GitHub link.

This paper extends the work of K. Takase on the rank of twists of local gamma factors for representations defined over a finite field of characteristic not equal to two. It examines unitary representations of a special orthogonal or symplectic group over the p-adic numbers, and investigates the relationship between the rank of twists of gamma factors and the isomorphism of representations. Specifically, for odd special orthogonal and symplectic groups, it proves that a certain number of twist ranks being less than zero implies the representations are isomorphic, and for the even special orthogonal group, it shows that the same conclusion holds under the condition that the representations have the same determinant. These results are achieved by building upon the methods introduced in Takase's previous research.

A graph G is considered Hamiltonian if it contains a Hamiltonian path, a sequence of connected vertices that visits every vertex in the graph. Building on this concept, G has a Hamiltonian path index if it contains a specific path that starts at a particular vertex and is essentially Hamiltonian. Then, G has a complete Hamiltonian path index if it contains a specific set of starting vertices that encompass the entire vertex set of G. Then, G has a complete Hamiltonian path index. In this paper, we investigate the Hamiltonian path index and complete Hamiltonian path index for various graph families, including circulant graphs, and some other types of graphs. We present efficient algorithms to determine the Hamiltonian path index for Cayley graphs and provide the Hamiltonian path index for certain graph families, such as Hamming graphs.

Researchers are still investigating the primary cell death mechanism resulting from SARS-CoV-2 infection. While apoptosis has been proposed, the involvement of pyroptosis and necroptosis is yet to be confirmed. Given that anti-inflammatory drugs have shown the ability to modify cell death from apoptosis to necroptosis in response to SARS-CoV-2 infection, pinpointing the exact cell death pathway is crucial. If necroptosis is the predominant cell death method induced by the virus, administering anti-inflammatory medications might prevent excessive inflammation and reduce mortality rates among COVID-19 patients.

This paper outlines three key advantages of algorithms that identify exogenous variables by breaking causal system equations into simpler components, which can be solved using smaller state-action spaces, enabling the use of smaller models, and yielding more efficient and manageable representations of problems.

In order to capitalize on these benefits, the article presents a methodical approach to identifying exogenous variables, and the results of an experiment demonstrate the method's effectiveness through application to a complex gridworld scenario, as well as the benefits it provides in terms of model size and computational efficiency compared to conventional methods.

Additionally, the article suggests that the approach to identifying exogenous variables can be integrated into structural causal models to facilitate the discovery of causal structures and interventions that lead to more efficient and manageable representations of problems.

The Michelson programming language is being utilized for the development of Ethereum contracts, and the HELMHOLTZ static analysis tool aids in Michelson program analysis. We have created an advanced Michelson compiler that compiles Michelson programs into a verified Python program, and we have applied this to significantly enhance HELMHOLTZ's verification capabilities. Our improvements include more precise gas error analysis for Michelson programs, more accurate uninitialized memory access error detection, and enhanced integer overflow analysis. Our evaluation shows that these enhancements provide better or equal performance compared to the existing analyses offered by HELMHOLTZ.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have significantly enhanced the capabilities of CNNs and FC-NNs, but these models often lack the ability to account for object relationships within an image. We propose a unified framework that integrates FC-NNs, CNNs, and object relationships into a single graph structure, enabling the use of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to enhance feature extraction and classification while maintaining compatibility with conventional deep learning architectures. We further extend this unification by showing how certain configurations of CNNs can be viewed as a form of GNN, and conversely, how GNNs can be expressed as a type of CNN. Lastly, we present GC3-Net, a GNN-based architecture that combines existing deep learning models by incorporating GNN layers as additional CNN layers.

We investigate a one-loop correction to the entropy of rotating "hairy" black holes in a 3D setting, where the modifications to gravity include the Chern-Simons term. By employing the entropy calculation method proposed by Witten, we compare our findings to those derived from the boundary central charge, the GSW surface method, and the entropy calculation of the CS theory. Although the entropy of these "hairy" black holes in a CS gravity is not directly calculable via a semi-classical approach due to the large N scaling, we demonstrate that the entropy of a "hairy" black hole in standard Chern-Simons gravity has the same value as that in pure gravity, which is more plausible physically. Additionally, we calculate a loop correction to the entropy of a rotating "hairy" black hole using the path integral approach proposed by Hartle and then confirm this result via the microscopic calculation of the entropy of the corresponding anti-de Sitter space with boundary conditions representing the black hole.

Recently, the focus has been on non-invertible symmetries beyond group theory, particularly those arising in quantum field theories. This is attributable to the ability of certain charge operators under global symmetries to detect defective operators with non-trivial topology. To address this, we adapt the categorical framework for non-invertible symmetries, utilizing Ext-objects to compute non-invertible charges and demonstrate their consistency with the fusion rules. This methodology is then applied to various theories, including free electric and magnetic theories, and theories with an $SU(N)$ symmetry, to explicitly derive the fusions of non-invertible symmetries in terms of their Ext-objects, thereby proving the ability of Ext-objects to capture the full structure of these symmetries, apart from the $U(1)$ charges.

The lateral and axial displacement estimations in ultrasound elastography (USE) are both critical, yet the latter exhibits significantly higher accuracy compared to the former. Improving lateral displacement estimation accuracy is essential for enhancing overall displacement estimation performance. This paper proposes a new training approach for lateral displacement estimation that builds upon the success of axial displacement estimation. Building upon the concept of tissue homogeneity, which suggests that local deformation is less complex than axial deformation, our method leverages the relationship between axial and lateral displacement gradients. By modeling the local relationship between these gradients, our proposed approach uses axial displacement estimation and its gradient as primary inputs to a regression network that predicts the lateral displacement. This approach is supported by both theoretical analysis and experimental evidence, which demonstrate its effectiveness in outperforming state-of-the-art methods on three publicly available datasets. Our proposed method exhibits notable improvements in lateral displacement estimation accuracy, resulting in enhanced overall displacement estimation performance.

Pseudocodes play a vital role in the cognitive process of problem-solving, problem-analysis, and problem-solving by computer scientists, enabling them to structure and organize their thoughts. Although pseudocodes are commonly used in these processes, there has been limited research on logically sound pseudocodes that can be verified for correctness and security, as well as automatically checked by composable proof assistants. In this research, we introduce a novel concept of a composable logical pseudocode, along with a framework for its automatic verification, in the context of dependent types. We demonstrate this framework by presenting a case study of a complex mathematical theorem that has been successfully proven using logical pseudocode. Our approach paves the way for the integration of composable logical pseudocodes into the computer-aided formalization and verification processes.

Given a fixed integer $r \ge 1$ and a sequence of positive integers
$n_1, n_2, \ldots, n_r$, we examine the Boolean rainbow Ramsey number
$RR(\binom{\cdot}{n_1}, \ldots, \binom{\cdot}{n_r})$ by considering a coloring
with $r$ distinct colors applied to the elements of the Boolean lattice
$2^{n_1} \uplus \ldots \uplus 2^{n_r}$. We aim to determine whether there
exists a sufficiently large integer $n$ such that the presence of a
union of $n_i$-dimensional Boolean lattices, each colored a different color,
is guaranteed within the colored lattice. Recent research has focused on
this topic, particularly by Kwan and Sawant in 2021 and Balogh, Jiang,
and Sawant in 2021. This paper contributes to the field by proving specific
results regarding the Boolean rainbow Ramsey number, initially by showing
subadditivity of the rainbow Ramsey number for a pair of intervals, and
later by establishing an inequality that places an upper limit on the
rainbow Ramsey number of a three-way colored union of intervals.

We present a novel one-pass coreset construction method for solving the $k$-means clustering problem with a given input dimension $d$. This co-core construction method, given an input stream of $n$ points and additional space of $\tilde{o}(n)$, efficiently produces a condensed representation. As a result, any $k$-means solution based on this representation is guaranteed to be within a factor $\tau$ of the optimal $k$-means cost scaled by a power of two. Our approach diverges from conventional techniques that rely on random sampling, utilizing a deterministic algorithm to achieve this end. Notably, our method establishes a coreset using $2^{O(k)} \cdot \mathrm{poly}(d, \tau)$ points in $O(1)$ passes, establishing $2^{O(k)}$ as the most efficient Coefficient (LCC) to date for this problem. Our method establishes this co-efficient through a combination of techniques, primarily leveraging an improved analysis of a data structure established by Fischer and Procaccia to address the problem of heavy hitters. Their structure, known as the KRR tree, facilitates finding approximations of low-rank vectors within a given dimension. We apply these approximations to construct coarser condensations from data streams in $O(1)$ time. Our algorithm establishes this co-core using $2^{O(k)} \cdot \mathrm{poly}(d, \tau)$ points in $O(1)$ passes,

In this scenario, we analyze the combination of two agents in a grid-based environment, where an evader seeks to avoid a pursuer. Computational metrics including time, grid size, and evader's starting positions affect scenario complexity. A method is proposed to minimize computational demands by grouping world states, which preserves optimal policy performance. A planning approach using this grouping concept allows for the development of a policy that surpasses value iteration in speed and generability. A method is also presented to quantify policy robustness, with results demonstrating the efficacy of this proposal.

A new class of nontransitive n-tuples based on rock-paper-scissors games has been introduced, specifically looking at RPS(G) games where G belongs to a set of groups. Properties of the RPS(G) games have been examined, with some members of this class already having been property tested. Additionally, a gradient modification has been implemented to check for symmetry-breaking, and it was found that most symmetry-breaking tests fail for games based on nontransitive (n, 3) tuples.

Our proposed enhancement to the cycleGAN framework involves the strategic incorporation of AdaIN components, a modification that significantly reduces the necessity for expansive data augmentations typically associated with image translation tasks. Rather than relying on conventional cycle-consistency and image reconstruction loss functions, a single AdaIN loss function was implemented to enforce consistency in feature representations across opposing translation directions. This method was initially evaluated on the challenging task of translating chest CT images to MRI, an example of a challenging translation between images that differ greatly in modality. The cycleAdaIN approach achieved superior results in this context, yielding enhanced image quality and improved segmentability of anatomical structures in comparison to both neighborhood embedding-based GAN models and conventional cycleGAN approaches.

In this study, we examine representations learned for multi-turn dialogues, with a focus on tasks requiring a thorough understanding of a turn from various perspectives, such as the dialog state prediction task. To achieve accurate predictions, a predictor must grasp the dialogue state mentioned in each utterance, its context within the preceding utterances, and the utterance's role in the dialogue flow. To assess the quality of these dialog representations, we compile a dataset called DialCorpus consisting of 12,000 dialogue pairs annotated with annotations on the utterance's preceding utterances, its mentioned dialogue states, and its utterance roles. To begin with, we devise a new scoring function across 12 dimensions that spans multi-turn dialogues and utilizes human judgments to assess this function. Notably, our model-based training using this function, called MultiViewLoss, results in representations that significantly enhance the dialog state prediction task's performance by 3.7%. By conducting a human evaluation and a set of dialog state prediction tasks, we conclude that our method successfully produces representations that capture utterance roles, utterance contexts, and dialogue states mentioned in the annotators' annotations. Lastly, to further validate our findings, we integrate annotators' dimensions into our model's loss function, called MetaLearningLoss, and our method's performance closely mirrors human judgments', with a correlation of 0.92.

In this research, we analyze a specific type of manifold, denoted as $M$, which involves a potential vector field $X$ and is related to a complex equation called the $\frac{\partial \mathcal{Y}}{\mathcal{t}}$-Ricci-Yamabe soliton equation. By examining this potential vector field, we aim to show that a certain derived equation, known as the Laplace equation, can result in multiple, distinct solutions. Additionally, we explore a specific type of manifold, called a gradient harmonic function soliton $\phi$-Ricci-Yamabe manifold, and demonstrate that under certain conditions, the function $u$ becomes constant. This research also touches on the potential existence of a certain type of soliton, known as the $\mathcal{Y}$-Ricci-Yamabe soliton, on a specific type of black hole, called a Kerr-Newman black hole.

A new approach to the geometry-based shell model is presented, specifically tailored for deformed halos. The method swiftly generates localized wave functions by leveraging rotational states derived from the geometry-based shell model in its single-particle picture. We successfully applied this approach to the $h_{11/2}$ neutron halo in $^{196}$Pb, accurately predicting a spatially distinct cluster and its orientation relative to the core. However, including the deformation of the core and the potential well shape, we found that the cluster's geometry, as well as the geometry-based shell model, could not entirely account for the localized structure observed in calculations based on the microscopic mean field.
Our proposed BasicVsr++ model significantly surpasses BasicVsr in performance, achieving a 0.55dB higher PSNR and utilizing 2x less computational power.

This study addresses the challenge of describing processes involving heavy vector bosons, such as W, Z, and Drell-Yan, at the parton level. An approach is introduced where the PDFs for these bosons are derived by solving the evolution equations of the DGLAP type and incorporating virtual corrections associated with collinear emissions. Notably, the computed corrections for these bosons demonstrate a pattern of alternation between positive and negative values, ultimately conforming to the universal corrections described by the CCFM equation for the corresponding partons in the high-x limit. As a result, the parton shower formalism can consistently incorporate processes involving these bosons by appending the appropriate virtual corrections, which were initially estimated using the derived PDFs for W, Z, or DY. This method has been implemented in the Pythia 8.3 Monte Carlo program through the activation of the corresponding Diabolo option.

In reinforcement learning, a common approach is to learn a model representing system dynamics. Researchers often propose learning shared models to facilitate simultaneous learning of multiple tasks. However, our investigation reveals that a single learned model can result in suboptimal or unstable policies in certain two-task scenarios. We identify two primary causes: model errors and insufficient exploration. To tackle this issue, we suggest learning separate models for each of the two tasks instead of a single shared model. Our findings demonstrate the superiority of our approach in multiple two-task scenarios. Moreover, we extend our method to successfully learn a single model for three or more tasks. Our contributions include both a theoretical and practical aspect: the first is a rigorous mathematical proof of the inability of shared models to accurately reflect real environments, while the second is an empirical evidence of algorithmical performance superiority in various two-task scenarios.

We establish an $L^2$-uniqueness result for a specific operator on a noncompact manifold, ensuring smooth edges, which aligns with previous findings for a plain space. Additionally, we demonstrate that this uniqueness may not hold without the $n \ge 3$ condition.

Godel's 1931 incompleteness theorem continues to be a subject of study and discussion. This ongoing interest is evident in the analysis of Godel's own views on the matter in his 1952 Princeton lectures. A key aspect of this discussion is Rosser's 1936 enhancement of the incompleteness principle. Building on the work of Godel, Gentzen, and others, D. Hilbert viewed mathematics through a foundational lens, seeking to establish a non-circular understanding of mathematical consistency. This paper explores the relationship between the incompleteness of formal systems and the limitations of foundational approaches, resulting in a negative conclusion to Hilbert's quest for a non-circular proof of mathematical consistency.

This study proposes novel upper bound formulas for the $L^2$-norms of evaluation functions at points situated between two circles in $(n+1)$-dimensional space, applicable to the monogenic function setting, where $n \geqslant 1$. Additionally, it discards the constraint of orthogonal functions from the monogenic function space and examines the rate of change of a monogenic function's $L^2$ norm across three circles or spheres of varying radii in $(n+1)$-dimensional space, while pinpointing two inner circles' radii and determining the relationship between their radiates and two critical parameters, $\lambda$ and \Lambda, that define the spectrum of the monogenic function space's boundary restriction operator.

When planning a survey, researchers often need to choose a balanced random sample from the population, constrained by available information about key variables. The author outlines three methods for selecting such variables, and focuses on one new method that uses an optimization approach to prioritize variables for balancing purposes. The proposed method ensures the selected variables can effectively balance a wide range of balanced sample options. To efficiently solve the resulting computational problem, the author suggests using a specific type of algorithm, and the effectiveness of this approach is evaluated using multiple examples. The results indicate that this method is highly effective at providing outcomes that can be easily worked with to achieve the desired balance across various variables.

Traditional robotics and vision systems rely on intermediate geometric representations of objects to perform complex tasks, which can be substitute directly with predictions, specifically through the use of regression models. Using this approach as a proof of concept, researchers have found that using direct regression to calibrate cameras in comparison to classical methods results in higher levels of accuracy. Furthermore, using an additional lens in the imaging pipeline does not produce a significant impact on the camera regression model's predictions, which in turn leads to the same levels of accuracy in task performance. Using this approach as a proof of concept, using this proof of concept results in the same levels of accuracy in task performance.

The task of inverse problem solving often requires generating multiple posterior samples under specific target distributions.  Another key challenge in deep generative adversarial network (GAN) research is accurately learning a target distribution.  We address these issues by proposing a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN (RCW-GAN) to efficiently produce posterior samples via a GAN framework.  We derive an objective function that combines a regularized inverse problem loss and a target GAN loss, allowing for a balanced learning process of the target GAN distribution.  We demonstrate the efficacy of RCW-GAN in various imaging tasks, including computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and diffusion-weighted imaging, through a series of experiments.  Notably, we show that even with a low GAN learning balance parameter, our method can accurately model the target tail of the posterior distribution while maintaining the ability to generate high-quality images.

This research provides a framework for analyzing time-varying fractional-order linear systems, drawing on recent developments in the theory of fractional calculus. Key concepts such as controllability, stabilizability, invariance of linear subspaces, and the calculation of system trajectories are defined and examined within this framework. Notably, the paper addresses a limitation in using the Caputo derivative for calculating system trajectories and introduces an alternative approach. Furthermore, the study establishes criteria for invariance in linear subspaces and comparisons to their time-invariant counterparts.

Building ultra-fast wireless networks in the terahertz range is made possible by multi-hop relay systems that can overcome severe signal blockages.  However, ensuring optimal alignment between transmitter and receiver antennas in these high-frequency systems demands a significant amount of time and energy for beam training.  By combining synchronized channel estimation and energy-efficient random access techniques, a novel beam training technique has been developed that minimizes the time and energy spent on finding the best transmitter-receiver antenna settings.  This new approach only requires the presence of a single temporary antenna setting at the relay node, and takes full advantage of the unique characteristics of multi-hop relay systems and relay node channel states.  Both theoretical calculations and simulated results confirm that the new beam training technique is vastly superior to current industry standards, achieving up to three times greater efficiency in terms of overhead.

The radio telescope observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, conducted from the Arecibo Observatory in 1973, revealed significant scintillation effects. These included the sudden changes in the scintillation pattern, which were attributed to the planet Neptune's influence on interstellar screens located between our solar system and the telescope at Arecibo. Analysis of the data revealed multiple individual scattering screens, consisting of distinct regions that caused diffraction patterns in the observations. Further analysis using a model of the system showed at least five separate screens, located at varying distances from our solar system. These findings have implications for the study of interstellar scintillation and the use of millimeter waves for communicating with extraterrestrial civilizations.

Recent advancements in deep learning have showcased the efficacy of cascaded networks in processing quasi-periodic signals, such as speech, by mirroring its inherent recursive structure. Utilizing a unified attention mechanism and a compact set of trainable parameters to capture long-range temporal dependencies within each processing stage, we developed a unified model with multiple, diverse attention heads in a cascaded structure. This unitary model was then integrated into a range of upstream tasks, and our experiments showed that it outperformed the current state-of-the-art models in robust speech recognition, particularly in noisy environments.
